World.title: Rob Manfred addresses possibility of cancelling 2027 Major League Baseball season: 'We want to play'
World.content:
The 2026 Major League Baseball season is rapidly drawing to a close, and there are multiple compelling storylines to follow.

Impressively, the American League is potentially set to make the wrong kind of history with several teams under .500 in postseason position. For once, there's a legitimate competition for National League MVP, with Cubs outfielder Pete Crow-Armstrong giving now-annual winner Shohei Ohtani a run for his money.

Speaking of Ohtani, his team, the Los Angeles Dodgers, have recovered from a lengthy losing streak to put themselves in position to secure a first round bye. As baseball's new villains, the Dodgers' fate in October will be the most talked about storyline. Win a third straight championship and fans, incorrectly, will complain about competitive balance in baseball. Lose in the NLDS or NLCS? They'll be "chokers" that deserve eternal scorn.

WITH ONE MONTH LEFT, AMERICAN LEAGUE TEAMS ARE HEADING TOWARDS AN EMBARRASSING, HISTORIC LOW

And that outcome might determine the likelihood of a 2027 season too. Not for any legitimate reason, but because the league's billionaire owners are committed to using misguided fan sentiment to push for their ultimate dream: increasing profits and reducing the percentage of revenue that goes to players through a salary cap. With the Collective Bargaining Agreement set to expire at the end of the year, there's a possibility, if not likelihood, that the owners lock the players out on December 1.

During Sunday night's Little League Classic game between the Atlanta Braves and Milwaukee Brewers, commissioner Rob Manfred joined the broadcast and wasn't exactly reassuring when talking about the possibility that the lockout could drag on well into the 2027 season.

MAJOR LEAGUE BASEBALL HAS A HUGE PROBLEM BREWING FOR THE 2026-2027 OFFSEASON

"We're meeting regularly, which is good," Manfred said during the ESPN broadcast. "Every week, we've had days where we've met with the players. It's early, but we've got a lot of work to do, and we're at it."

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Sounds good, right? Meetings are happening. Conversations are happening. Maybe there's hope. Well, about that.

"Look, our goal is to make a deal. We want to make a deal. We want to play baseball next year. We're planning on playing baseball next year," Manfred said.

"We want," is not "we will." "We're planning" is also not "we will."

WORLD SERIES CHAMPION JOHN SMOLTZ WARNS MLB 'CANNOT AFFORD' A WORK STOPPAGE WITH CBA SET TO EXPIRE

Obviously, the two sides are engaged in active negotiations, and as such, Manfred may not want to weaken his bargaining position by giving too much away. He's also smart enough to know the position baseball is in right now, with attendance and ratings growing and the Dodgers giving the other 29 fanbases a compelling foil.

But it's still a bit disconcerting to hear "want" and "planning" when the future popularity of the sport is at stake. Baseball can't afford a lengthy work stoppage or, God forbid, the cancellation of the 2027 season. Young, exciting players like Crow-Armstrong, Bobby Witt Jr., Konnor Griffin, Paul Skenes, Jacob Misiorowski, Junior Caminero, Jordan Walker, Gunnar Henderson, J.J. Wetherholt and Kevin McGonigle are helping the league build momentum.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Losing out on a year of development, growth, and excitement is simply not an option. Hopefully Manfred realizes that, public comments aside.

World.title: More details about Jed York's arrest in a prostitution sting come to light and begs questions about the 49ers
World.content:
More details continue to pour in about the "engaging in prostitution" arrest charges and subsequent conviction on lesser charges of San Francisco 49ers majority owner Jed York.

York was arrested in his native Ohio on Sunday on one charge of "engaging in prostitution" and another charge of "possessing criminal tools." And while the more salacious charge was downgraded to "disorderly conduct" in a plea deal with the prosecutor, it is that initial charge on which York was arrested and arraigned that sticks in the minds fans, media, everybody.

It's the embarrassing charge that raises eyebrows because York is reportedly worth $500 million and the family fortune is believed to hover around $8.5 billion, but he allegedly tried to enlist the services of a prostitute for $140.

49ERS OWNER JED YORK ARRESTED FOR 'ENGAGING IN PROSTITUTION' IN OHIO, PLEADS NO CONTEST TO LESSER CHARGES

Did we tell you that York's legal team immediately filed a motion to seal court records?

The motion was denied.

And so here comes the details not in the original OutKick story that have since come to light via reporting:

York responded to an  on Sunday from what police say is a known prostitution website in Columbiana County, Ohio. He allegedly "arranged to have sexual activity with a female in exchange for $140," per police.

The meeting with the prostitute was supposed to happen near the Wheat Hill Mobile Home Community – a trailer park in East Palestine, Ohio.

In fact, York had fallen for a police sting by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force and the NFL owner was intercepted by officers when he approached the trailer park.

FLORIDA ATTORNEY GENERAL SUBPOENAS NFL AS PART OF NEW PROBE INTO ROONEY RULE AND OTHER DEI PROGRAMS

York was taken into custody by the East Palestine police.

The mobile home park, by the way, claims it is a victim of circumstances. It's Facebook account posted that Park addresses were not being used in the sting operation, but rather that's where cops happened to catch up to York.

"This news of this arrest in our quiet community is just as shocking to us as to the rest of you," the post reads.

York was taken into custody when he was found in possession of the cell phone that was used to set up the alleged rendezvous with the person he allegedly believed to be a hooker.

The phone in York's possession "was used to arrange the criminal act," according to court records and that is the reason he was also charged with "possessing criminal tools."

York pleaded no contest to the misdemeanor plea deal charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools, per court records.

The NFL previously told OutKick that this matter will be reviewed by the league under the Personal Conduct Policy.

In 2014, the NFL updated its conduct policy and specifically warned those beyond the field that it applies to them.

BRANDON AIYUK'S SOCIAL MEDIA POST MOCKING KYLE SHANAHAN'S CAR CRASH DRAWS BACKLASH AND COULD COST HIM A JOB

"It is a privilege to be part of the National Football League," the policy states. "Everyone who is part of the league must refrain from conduct detrimental to the integrity of and public confidence in the NFL. This includes owners, coaches, players, other team employees, game officials, and employees of the league office, NFL Films, NFL Network or any other NFL business."

The policy also leaves little room to question whether York will simply walk away from this incident without a penalty from the league.

"If you are convicted of a crime or subject to a disposition of a criminal proceeding, you are subject to discipline," the policy states. "But even if your conduct does not result in a criminal conviction, if the league finds that you have engaged in conduct [prohibited by the policy], you will be subject to discipline."

York got arrested. He pleaded no contest on two criminal charges. And he has brought negative attention to the NFL.

The 49ers on Monday declined to comment on the York arrest and plea deal, citing the episode is closed.

But this won't be over until the NFL rules.

World.title: Syria off US terror blacklist after nearly 50 years as Trump admin clears investment hurdle
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The United States on Monday formally removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a move Secretary of State Marco Rubio said eliminates the final major barriers to investment and economic recovery in the country.

Rubio said in a statement that he had authorized the formal rescission after a mandatory 45-day congressional notification period ended.

President Donald Trump had initiated the countdown in July after confirming to Congress that Syria’s government had ceased supporting acts of international terrorism.

"I have also delisted Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham’s (HTS) designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT)," Rubio said Monday.

FORMER ASSAD-ERA PRISON CHIEF CONVICTED OF TORTURE IN US FEDERAL COURT, MARKING A HISTORIC FIRST

The actions, he said, represent "another historic step by President Trump to give the Syrian people a path to prosperity."

Rubio said Washington had taken unprecedented steps over the past year to provide sanctions relief to the Syrian people.

He pointed to Trump’s June 2025 executive order, "Providing for the Revocation of Syria Sanctions," which accelerated sanctions relief by terminating the Syria Sanctions Program and the national emergency with respect to Syria while directing reviews of other Syria-related sanctions and terrorist designations.

"These actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism," Rubio said of the Syrian government.

Al-Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024 in an offensive led by HTS rebels. Syria had been on the State Sponsors of Terrorism list since 1979, with the designation in force throughout al-Assad’s rule.

BRIEF ALCOHOL BAN IN DAMASCUS SPARKS CONCERNS ABOUT PRESIDENT AL-SHARAA'S VISION FOR SYRIA

"In the past year, the Government of Syria has taken significant steps to counterterrorism, to include formally joining the Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS in November and conducting operations to disrupt the terror networks of ISIS, al-Qa’ida, Hizballah, and Iran-aligned groups," Rubio said.

He added that rescinding Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism and HTS’ designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist "eliminates the final major barriers for private-sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria’s economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy."

EVANGELICAL LEADER SAYS US MUST PROTECT SYRIAN CHRISTIANS FROM ATTACKS BY JIHADI TERRORISTS

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani told Reuters on Aug. 22 that lifting the designation would help restore Syria’s links to the global financial system and encourage investment following nearly 14 years of war.

"There is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria," he said.

"Today’s action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said in a statement, adding that it is "in line with President Trump’s promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria."

The governor of the Central Bank of Syria said Monday that lifting Syria’s designation as a state sponsor of terrorism is a "historic step that returns it to its natural place within the global economic system."

On Monday, Trump also posted a photo on Truth Social of al-Sharaa and al-Shibani holding his signed June 2025 executive order directing sanctions relief for Syria.

Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries designated by Washington as state sponsors of terrorism.

World.title: Trump admin eyes historic mass visa revocation targeting up to 200K asylum seekers: report
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration is reportedly preparing to revoke business and tourist visas held by as many as 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum in the U.S.

The State Department is expected to announce the sweeping action in the coming weeks, The Associated Press reported, citing internal documents and two U.S. officials.

The effort would target B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to foreigners who later sought asylum. If carried out, the move would mark the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history and could face legal challenges, according to the outlet.

FOREIGN DRUNK DRIVERS COULD FACE SWIFT BOOT OUT OF COUNTRY UNDER TRUMP'S 'AMERICA FIRST' CRACKDOWN

"We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

Pigott did not confirm how many people could be affected, saying the revocations would occur on a "rolling basis" and the total remained "dynamic," according to the AP.

The move would not automatically lead to immediate deportations.

Foreigners with pending asylum cases would generally be reclassified but would lose their status as business or tourist travelers, officials told the AP.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau said Monday that asylum should not be used to bypass immigration laws.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Landau wrote on X. "Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

TRUMP TELLS FOREIGN STUDENTS: OVERSTAY YOUR VISA, FACE THE CONSEQUENCES

B1 visas are typically issued for business travel, while B2 visas cover tourism, family visits and medical care. Currently, applicants must demonstrate that they plan to return to their home countries.

The potential revocations come as the Trump administration cracks down on what it considers abuse of the immigration system. The State Department has revoked roughly 175,000 visas over the past 18 months, according to The Associated Press.

The State Department could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Ex-NBA player tells Laura Ingraham why WNBA can't ban him: 'I identify as a woman'
World.content:
Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom joined Laura Ingraham on "The Ingraham Angle" Monday night to set the record straight following his chaotic courtside ejection from Sunday's Indiana Fever-Chicago Sky matchup.

Freedom was escorted out of Wintrust Arena late in the third quarter after Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud unleashed an explicit, profanity-laced tirade against him after simply celebrating a 3-pointer by Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Freedom, who sat baseline wearing a shirt defining "woman" as an "adult human female," explained to Ingraham that he attended purely out of love for basketball and to back Cunningham, an athlete who has faced relentless backlash for defending female sports.

ENES KANTER FREEDOM MET WITH HOSTILE WNBA FANS EN ROUTE TO FEVER-SKY MATCHUP

But after Freedom put his hands up following a made bucket, Cloud immediately confronted him with personal insults, mocking and screaming that Cunningham was "not going to sleep" with him.

"I actually loved the game and enjoyed the game," Freedom told Ingraham.

"This is my passion... first half I watched the game; it was an amazing time. They put Sophie Cunningham in. I remember around the last three-minute mark she shot the ball and I put my hand in the air to celebrate it. Then Natasha Cloud saw that. Literally the next possession, (Cloud) came back and yelled at me, '(Sophie Cunningham) is not going to sleep with you.'"

Freedom admitted the outburst left him stunned.

PAYTON MCNABB: THE BACKLASH AGAINST SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM PROVES THE GOALPOSTS HAVE MOVED

"I'm just confused at that point," Freedom said. "I'm here to protect women and support Sophie Cunningham."

Cloud escalated the confrontation with a slew of F-bombs in front of a section filled with young children, Kanter noted.

"The next possession, (Cloud) started to yell and cuss at me," Freedom said.

"I was like, there are so many kids in those stands. There are so many teenagers... a lot of F-bombs. She started to come toward me and I literally got up... I'm like, what did I do? She should be the one to be thrown out of the game."

SKY COACH PRAISES NATASHA CLOUD AFTER HEATED VERBAL ALTERCATION WITH ENES KANTER FREEDOM

Instead of penalizing Cloud for charging at Enes and dropping vulgarities, arena security escorted Freedom out of the building.

Enes’ shirt has apparently become kryptonite for a WNBA still unable to answer the most basic question in women’s sports.

What is a woman?

"I'm shocked it's a controversial topic nowadays, but it is," Freedom noted.

After Enes' appearance on Sunday, the league sneakily drew a line in the sand, telling media outlets like Front Office Sports that Kanter Freedom will not be eligible to get drafted into the WNBA.

He reminded them of their loose standard of what a woman is.

"I am a woman. I should be allowed to play," Kanter told Ingraham. "Article 13 Section 1 says if you identify as a woman, then you are allowed to play. I identify as a woman, so yes I can play."

"They're terrified because I might actually get drafted next year."

Enes' primetime appearance comes as former NBA pick Royce White warned the WNBA will likely attempt to ban Freedom from future games to protect themselves on a PR level and dodge further scrutiny over its gender policies.

While Fever head coach Stephanie White tried to play media gatekeeper postgame by labeling the chaos a mere "social media thing," Freedom's interview proves the opposite.

World.title: John Harbaugh calls it 'reasonable to assume' Malik Nabers will be available for Giants in Week 1 vs Cowboys
World.content:
Malik Nabers has shocked many New York Giants fans in training camp with just how great he looks on the gridiron with his teammates after an offseason shrouded in mystery and doubt about whether he’d be ready for Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys on "Sunday Night Football."

Now, after practicing without a red non-contact jersey Monday, head coach John Harbaugh gave yet another encouraging update on the Giants 2024 first-round pick that points in the right direction for his availability to start the season.

Harbaugh told reporters Monday that it is "reasonable to assume" Nabers is trending toward being available right out the gate for the Giants, which is an incredible sign for the wide receiver who tore his right ACL and had meniscus damage in Week 4 last season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"Probably moving the best we’ve seen him look," Harbaugh said about Nabers, as he wore a regular white jersey alongside his fellow receivers during 11-on-11 and 7-on-7 reps on Monday.

In fact, Harbaugh believes that "very reasonable" contact with defenders during practice is something he’d be fine seeing Nabers go through.

ODELL BECKHAM TOLD GIANTS COACH HE'S READY TO 'GO OUT ON MY SWORD' TO EARN ROSTER SPOT

"Those are all kind of things that you can assume," Harbaugh said when asked about Nabers in terms of Week 1 availability. "It’s just based on watching the guy practice. The only thing I know more than you guys know is what the docs and the trainers tell me, as far as his rehab. And that’s doing well. He’s doing really well with that. He’s strong. He’s in a good place."

It wasn’t a fully padded practice for the Giants, but Nabers has been spotted wearing the red non-contact uniform for quite a bit now.

Seeing Nabers not wearing the non-contact jersey, though, is exactly what Harbaugh had planned for the team’s top pass-catching option. He noted not wanting to see Nabers go from no contact to 100% to start the season.

And for Nabers himself, he said last week "my soul has been dead for so long," hinting at how badly he’s wanted to get back on the field and do what he loves. He also noted the "dog" in him is starting to wake up, and he’s only been trending in an upward trajectory since that first training camp practice surprised fans with just how well he was moving in and out of his routes.

Now, it shouldn’t be expected that Nabers gets time in the Giants’ final preseason game against the New York Jets this week. The teams won’t be holding any joint practices either, so Nabers’ journey to Week 1 availability will have to continue against his teammates.

But the build is there, and the LSU product continues to check boxes in his new head coach’s head.

"I thought he looked good. Look at the tape later, but he was moving well. …It was a good practice for him today," Harbaugh said.

Nabers and quarterback Jaxson Dart have developed quite the chemistry already, but the Giants’ 2025 draft choice out of Ole Miss only had one quarter with Nabers during his first career start before the devastating knee injury.

World.title: Supreme Court hands preliminary win to Trump on mail-in ballots executive order
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration Monday in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

At issue are provisions that seek to create a federal list of eligible voters and order the U.S. Postal Service to deliver ballots only to those people.

The justices, divided 6-3 along ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, lifted an injunction a Massachusetts-based judge imposed in June that prevented key aspects of the executive order from going into effect this year in California and 22 other states that had challenged it.

The court also granted a similar application filed by Alabama and 11 other states.

The White House praised the court’s ruling, calling the executive order’s provisions “commonsense measures.”

“This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement.

U.S. Postal Service headquarters in Washington. Erin Scott / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Parts of the same executive order are blocked nationwide because of a ruling the same judge issued later in a different case, but the Supreme Court decision is likely to apply to that ruling, too.

That means the administration may, at least in the short term, be able to implement the executive order, but the legal battle is far from over.

“This decision is a painful setback, but it will not be the final word,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among those who challenged the proposal, said in a statement.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, said Monday night that his state will launch a new challenge to the Trump administration’s policy on mail-in voting.

“Following today’s SCOTUS ruling, California WILL SUE again to BLOCK Trump’s attack on mail-in voting!” Newsom said on X. “Every eligible voter gets a mail-in ballot here — and we’ll fight to keep it that way.”

President Donald Trump has frequently railed against the widespread use of mail-in ballots as part of his broader complaints, offered without evidence, that the election system is plagued with fraud.

His efforts to encourage Congress to pass his SAVE America Act legislation that would impose new voting restrictions nationwide, including proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter ID, have so far failed.

Election workers process mail-in ballots at San Francisco County's election operations facility at City Hall in San Francisco in June. David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

The Supreme Court decision is provisional, focusing only on the argument that U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani acted prematurely in preventing the provisions from being implemented in the 23 states before federal agencies had even drawn up plans for how to implement the executive order.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned ruling.

The decision leaves the door open to judges’ intervening later, especially with regard to any restrictions imposed for the coming midterm elections. On Friday, while the case was pending, the Postal Service issued its final regulation that would enforce parts of the executive order.

The dissenters were the three liberal justices on the conservative-majority court.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful. Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote.

In a separate dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson accused the majority of “taking its eye off the ball” by focusing on a technical legal argument instead of what she views as the larger goal of the Trump administration: “to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.”

The Trump administration told the Supreme Court the new regulations did not go as far as the executive order anticipated, saying the Postal Service “will not refuse to transmit ballots” even if senders are not on a state list of registered voters.

The Supreme Court decision is in line with one in a related case by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that rejected a separate attempt by Democrats to block the executive order.

Lower courts declined to put the Massachusetts ruling on hold, leading the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the filing that it was premature for courts to rule on the issue, as neither the Postal Service nor other agencies have determined how they will implement the executive order. It would be a tall order for the chronically underfunded Postal Service, with just months to go before Election Day.

World.title: California attorney general cancels talks with Paramount, accuses company of leaks
World.content:
California’s attorney general called off a meeting Monday with Paramount Skydance to discuss a potential settlement of the state’s antitrust lawsuit seeking to block the media company’s $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery.

In a statement Monday morning, California Attorney General Rob Bonta confirmed he “pulled down this meeting” and accused Paramount of “playing games.”

“I prefer to resolve disputes in the boardroom, not the courtroom. As I’ve also said, if the opposing party in litigation wants to meet in good faith to make a sincere effort to resolve the case, we’ll meet,” Bonta said in part.

Bonta accused Paramount of leaking “the alleged substance of settlement discussions” that were held on Friday. “But they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the Democratic official added.

A Paramount water tower; California Attorney General Rob Bonta. Getty Images file

In response to a request for comment Monday, a spokesperson for Paramount said the company shared Bonta’s “concerns about the public discussions and misreporting that has surrounded this deal.”

“As we have assured the Attorney General’s office, Paramount has not been the source of the leaks of any of our confidential discussions with the AG’s office,” the Paramount spokesperson added.

Bonta and the Paramount spokesperson appeared to be referring to a Wall Street Journal article published Saturday that detailed some of the conversation topics at Friday’s meeting.

The back-and-forth is the latest twist in a corporate saga that has riveted Hollywood in recent months.

Twelve state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America filed a lawsuit last month challenging the tie-up between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of the country’s leading entertainment and media conglomerates.

The states contend the deal violates federal antitrust law and threatens to “extinguish” economic competition in three markets: wide-release theatrical films, anticipated top-grossing movies and basic cable television distribution.

Paramount has flatly rejected those claims, calling the states’ lawsuit “wrong on both the facts and the law.” It has argued that the merger will increase economic competition and production output across film and television.

The company has agreed to freeze the merger until either the antitrust challenge is resolved or June 1, 2027 — whichever comes first. Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is presiding over the case, scheduled an antitrust trial for early March.

Paramount has already won clearance from the Department of Justice and secured regulatory go-aheads from more than 60 territories around the world, including Australia, China and the European Union.

The combined corporation would be led by David Ellison, the 43-year-old son of Oracle mogul Larry Ellison. It would encompass two movie studios, two streaming platforms, a suite of cable channels and two marquee news organizations: CBS News and CNN.

Ellison has threatened to move Paramount out of its traditional headquarters in California unless Bonta opened settlement talks, according to a source who was in a closed-door meeting earlier this month but wasn’t authorized to speak about it on the record.

If the deal hasn’t closed by Oct. 1, according to the companies’ agreement, Paramount will be on the hook for a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. shareholders, or roughly $650 million a quarter.

California political leaders have urged both sides in the legal conflict to get to a resolution.

“The continued uncertainty is not good for the workers, not good for productions and not good for the future of this industry,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat running for re-election, said last week.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed concerns that the antitrust challenge could harm California employment if the deal is blocked.

In response to NBC News’ request for comment on that report, Newsom’s office said it “doesn’t comment on anonymous sources or unverified reporting.”

In the antitrust challenge, California is joined by the Democratic attorneys general of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington.

World.title: As Ukraine’s allies gather for big anniversary, one key backer is absent
World.content:
Leaders of Ukraine’s international allies on Monday marked 35 years since the country broke away from the Soviet Union to become an independent nation.

The U.K.’s Andy Burnham flew in, while France’s Emmanuel Macron and Germany’s Friedrich Merz joined a call to reaffirm commitments to Kyiv.

But senior officials from one longtime backer were notably absent from the public show of support: the United States.

While U.S. senators and former officials visited Ukraine ahead of the commemorations, the apparent lack of senior Trump administration participation was the latest sign of how Washington has backed off during a critical juncture for Ukraine.

The message sent was especially pointed as Monday also marks 4 1/2 years since President Vladimir Putin launched his large-scale invasion of Russia’s much smaller neighbor.

Negotiations to reach a peace deal, which President Donald Trump once promised to achieve within 24 hours, have stalled as supplies of U.S. air defense missiles dwindle and the Russian leader ramps up threats to Ukraine’s allies.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, center left, and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, center right, in Kyiv on Monday. Henry Nicholls / Getty Images

Britain’s Burnham was the highest-profile Western leader to fly in and co-chair a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of countries backing Ukraine.

European Council President António Costa, as well as the heads of nearly a dozen European nations, was also in Kyiv, despite the country’s air force reporting Russian rocket and drone strikes overnight.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Ukraine in a statement.

“The United States is committed to Ukraine’s sovereignty and continues to work to support a negotiated settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war that establishes a lasting and durable peace,” it said.

World.title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
World.content:
GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.

Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.

“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”

Lifelong Gary, Ind., resident Joetta Walker, 73, holds her nebulizer. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.

“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.

As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.

Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”

Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”

“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.

Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.

“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.

Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.

“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Tree Care workers from Michigan remove a tree from the front of a home in Gary on Thursday after it was toppled during a recent storm. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”

On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.

“All gone, gone,” she said.

At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

Walker stands in front of her empty fridge, where, she says, more than $700 worth of food has spoiled. Selina Guevara / NBC News

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”

Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.

“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.

In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.

“It’s been crazy,” he said.

Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.

“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”

Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.

“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.

“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.

Channie Weaver, 50, of Gary. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.

“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”

Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.

“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.

Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

World.title: Jared Kushner and Hakeem Jeffries met as midterm elections loom
World.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and President Trump's adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner met recently, a source familiar with the details confirmed to CBS News.

The private discussion comes less than three months before the midterms. Democrats are aiming to take control of the House in the November elections, with Jeffries in line to possibly become the next House Speaker if they win the majority. It also comes as Republicans — led by Mr. Trump — have cast Democrats as the party of dangerous extremes.

The New York Times first reported the meeting, which took place in New York City and covered a broad range of topics and potential areas of common ground such as housing, immigration and cost of living. The White House and a Kushner spokesperson did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment.

Jeffries confirmed the meeting in a social media video late Monday, saying Kushner "asked for a meeting, and I took it to discuss the affordability crisis."

"I shouldn't have to say it, but I am: No one is going to get a pass. We're going to hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable, beginning on day one," Jeffries added.

In a statement over the weekend, Jeffries said Democrats will not tolerate Republicans' "my-way-or-the-highway approach to governing that has failed the American people."

"To stop the madness, we have repeatedly made clear that an extremist approach will not work and will be met with forceful opposition," Jeffries said.

Kushner has no formal role in the White House, but he serves as a key adviser to Mr. Trump in overseas diplomatic negotiations. He and Jeffries worked together on criminal justice reform legislation during Mr. Trump's first term.

House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday that he first learned of this meeting from news reports.

"I don't know what that's about," Johnson said to Fox News' Peter Doocy. "I know Jared has interests and lots of other things going on. He's not really directly involved in the admin, at least in the day-to-day in the White House."

While Mr. Trump met frequently with Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and the former House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi in his first term, he has only met with Schumer and Jeffries once so far this term.

Mr. Trump has instead used his social media to insult both of them, including referring to Jeffries as "low IQ" and a "thug." Earlier this year, Jeffries called Mr. Trump "the dumbest president ever."

However, in an interview this month with Punchbowl News, Mr. Trump said he could work with the Democratic leader and described him as a "nice guy."

"People are harsh on me. I'm harsh on them. It's part of the world," Mr. Trump said. "I'd probably get along with him very well."

World.title: Former Stars and Stripes editor says firing was a "real shock"
World.content:
Days after his sudden firing by the Pentagon, the former editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes told CBS News that "time will tell" whether the military newspaper will remain editorially independent from the government agency it covers.

The Defense Department delivered termination notices last week to Stars and Stripes Editor-in-Chief Erik Slavin, publisher Max Lederer and Middle East reporter Lara Korte, accusing them of insubordination. The dismissals raised questions about the future of the paper, which is partly funded by U.S. taxpayers but has historically operated independently.

In an interview Monday on CBS News' "The Takeout with Major Garrett," Slavin called the termination notice a "real shock" and a "very unexpected" development. Slavin had worked at the Stars and Stripes for just over two decades, serving as a reporter and bureau chief before being promoted to editor-in-chief last fall.

The stated reason for his firing, Slavin said, was his appearance last month in a "CBS Sunday Morning" report on the Trump administration's push to overhaul Stars and Stripes. Slavin was asked if there were any lines that he would not cross, and he said a demand from the military not to publish a "perfectly accurate story" would be a "red line."

On Monday, Slavin called those comments a "hypothetical response, in my personal opinion, as to what would be my red line. And I described censorship, which I believe to be in line with Department of Defense regulations and the law itself."

Stars and Stripes was first published during the Civil War, and in recent decades, the paper has prided itself on its editorial independence — meaning the federal government does not dictate what it can and can't publish.

Roughly half of Stars and Stripes' $29 million annual budget comes from taxpayers, a person familiar with the newspaper's operations told CBS News last week. Readership has declined since its peaks during the Vietnam War, the Cold War and World War II, according to two U.S. officials, but an average of 1.4 million people see Stars and Stripes each day. Print editions overseas also reach service members in remote locations.

Slavin described the paper's goal as giving service members "the straight truth."

"They hold us accountable every day," Slavin said of the paper's readers. "If we get something that doesn't correspond with their lived experience, they call us out on it real fast."

"We never think, really, in terms of positive and negative, but I can certainly see why maybe the Pentagon would. But we don't shy away from that, we look for what's new, different, interesting and relevant to service members," he added.

Earlier this year, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said the Defense Department would make sweeping changes to the paper. He vowed to "modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members." The Pentagon later sought to stop the paper from running syndicated articles by wire services, Slavin has said.

Last week, Lederer told colleagues he planned to retire at the end of September, citing fundamental differences with the Trump administration. And on Friday, Lederer, Slavin and Korte were terminated.

Slavin told CBS News: "I certainly hope [Stars and Stripes] can remain independent in some way. I haven't given up on that, but time will tell, and I think there needs to be a reckoning."

Shortly after the firings, Stars and Stripes published an open letter from Navy Capt. William Urban, who said he was tapped to serve as military deputy to the publisher. Urban wrote that his priorities were to produce "the highest quality of editorially independent reporting," while modernizing the paper and boosting its advertising revenue.

Asked about Urban's letter and his pledge to keep the paper independent, Slavin said he's "not sure" how to square it with this year's push to change the paper's operations.

Korte — the Middle East reporter who was fired alongside Slavin for sitting for a "CBS Sunday Morning" interview — said in a separate interview with CBS News on Monday that she has "certainly been bolstered to see comments from the Stripes' leadership and from the Pentagon that the Stripes is editorially independent."

"Obviously that's something that has to be instituted in practice, and I think that's something we're going to get an answer on in the coming weeks and months," she said.

The Pentagon has made other changes to how the military can be covered.

Last year, reporters who cover the Pentagon were told that in order to maintain daily access to the building, they would need to sign on to a host of rules, including a restriction on "soliciting" sensitive information from military personnel. CBS News and many other media outlets declined to sign the policy, leading dozens of reporters to turn in their press credentials. The Pentagon has denied that it is seeking to control what reporters can publish, calling the rules necessary to prevent harmful leaks.

A judge struck down many of the new rules earlier this year, and the military replaced them with a requirement that all journalists be escorted while inside the Pentagon.

Slavin told CBS News that "there used to be a time … where in the Pentagon, it was very simple for military officials to talk with journalists very frankly."

"I think it contributed to the nation's knowledge of what the U.S. military was doing, and I fear that we're losing that," he said.

World.title: Ex-NBA center ejected from WNBA game after being confronted by player
World.content:
Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night's Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, 34, as she approached him. Video showed a standing Kanter holding his arms out and taking one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom and Natasha Cloud #9 of the Chicago Sky yell at one another during the second half between the Chicago Sky and the Indiana Fever at Wintrust Arena on Aug. 23, 2026, in Chicago. Michael Reaves/Getty Images

"There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we're just going to focus on the game," Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky's 113-90 loss.

Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.

"I told her she wasn't," Marsh said. "I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash."

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

"I didn't see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle," Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, "so I think that's probably a question for Chicago."

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls' and women's sports. Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.

Kanter, a native of Turkey who became a U.S. citizen in 2021, joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.

"If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball," he said, "and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too."

Cloud did not speak with the media after Sunday's game, CBS Sports reported. She later made a statement on social media.

"To every trans kid/person, You are apart of MY community & tribe. You belong. You're loved. You're seen. You're perfect as you are. & you will always be protected by me," Cloud wrote.

This is not the first time Cloud and Kanter Freedom have crossed paths. In 2023, the two went back and forth on social media after Cloud criticized the U.S. government.

World.title: Supreme Court allows Trump to implement parts of order restricting mail voting
World.content:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday allowed President Trump's administration to move ahead with implementing key portions of an executive order that seeks to tighten the rules for mail voting ahead of the November midterm elections.

In a 6-3 ruling, the high court granted a request for emergency relief sought by the Trump administration late last month in a case involving 23 Democratic-led states. The Justice Department had asked the Supreme Court to lift a lower court's injunction that stopped agencies from carrying out parts of Mr. Trump's directive, which involves the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Postal Service, in those states and the District of Columbia.

The high court said in its unsigned decision that the states filed their lawsuit too soon.

"The Court's disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful," the Supreme Court said in an unsigned decision. "On that score, time will tell. But the Order itself does not harm the States, so the District Court lacked jurisdiction to bar the Government from trying to implement it."

The move from the high court clears the way for the Department of Homeland Security to move forward with a proposal to create lists of residents in each state who are eligible to vote.

The White House called the decision "a major win for the security of American elections."

"These are commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on - which includes the safety and security of our elections."

In a separate case involving voting-rights groups, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani issued an order earlier this month that prevents the Trump administration from implementing the executive order's provisions that direct the Postal Service to develop new procedures for mail ballots for the upcoming elections. But the Justice Department will likely argue the Supreme Court's decision applies to that case, too.

The emergency appeal before the Supreme Court, meanwhile, arose after Talwani sided with the group of states that challenged Mr. Trump's executive order and ruled the Constitution does not grant the president the authority to order changes to how they administer federal elections.

The Supreme Court's order does not preclude the states from filing lawsuits that challenge the policies finalized and ultimately put in place by the administration in response to Mr. Trump's directive. Some states are set to begin sending mail ballots to voters for the upcoming midterms in the coming weeks.

The three liberal justices dissented from the Supreme Court's ruling. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Elena Kagan, noted that the decision "merely postpones adjudication" of challenges to Mr. Trump's policies.

"Today's decision does not address whether the President's attempts to interfere with States' administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful," Sotomayor wrote in a dissenting opinion. "Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President's directives."

Trump's executive order

Since returning to the White House for his second term, Mr. Trump has sought to exert control over aspects of federal elections. As part of those efforts, the president signed in March an executive order that he said aims to protect the integrity of U.S. elections in part by ensuring noncitizens are not casting ballots. Mr. Trump's directive came just months before the November midterm elections, which will determine which party controls the House and Senate.

The provisions at issue in the case direct DHS to compile "state citizenship lists" using federal databases and call for the Postal Service to deliver mail ballots cast only by individuals who are on its own voter-eligibility lists. The directive also lays out certain design requirements for mail ballot envelopes and instructs the attorney general to prioritize investigations and prosecutions of state and local officials who issue ballots to noncitizens or others who are not eligible to vote in federal elections.

The Postal Service published a final rule Friday putting in place some of the plans laid out in Mr. Trump's executive order. The rule lays out required design elements for federal mail ballot envelopes and directs state election officials to submit specific data to an online portal, including the names and addresses of voters they intend to send mail ballots to.

Using that information, the Postal Service will then generate and send state-specific "Mail-In and Absentee Participation Lists" to states' chief election officials on Election Day. The new rule said the lists are "primarily intended to assist election officials and law enforcement to understand who may have been mailed a ballot, in order to identify potentially anomalous incidents that may merit further investigation."

The Postal Service "will not play any role in determining voter eligibility, maintaining voter rolls, or counting ballots," it said.

The agency said it would act immediately to implement the new rule for the November midterms once the government obtained relief from lower-court injunctions.

The legal challenge to Trump's directive

Days after the president signed the executive order in March, Democratic officials from the 23 states and D.C. filed a lawsuit seeking to block the proposals. The states argued that the president has no power to restrict voter eligibility or mail voting, and said the executive order attempts to interfere with their administration of elections in violation of the Constitution.

A separate group of 12 Republican-led states intervened in the lawsuit and, with the Trump administration, argued it should be dismissed.

But Talwani ruled in June that under the Constitution, only the states determine voter-eligibility requirements, and the president lacks any role in that area. The judge held that the provisions of the executive order governing DHS and the Postal Service are unconstitutional, and she blocked the Trump administration from implementing those portions for the Nov. 3 elections in the 23 states that sued.

The Justice Department appealed the ruling, arguing that the states' lawsuit is premature. But in a 2-1 decision late last month, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit declined to let federal agencies move forward with implementing Mr. Trump's executive order as litigation continues.

The Trump administration then asked the Supreme Court to intervene. The Justice Department called the district court's injunction "extraordinary" and "indefensible" because federal agencies are still considering how to implement the president's executive order.

In filings with the high court, Solicitor General D. John Sauer did not defend the legal merits of the president's plans. Instead, he argued that the 23 states filed their lawsuit too soon. Federal agencies, Sauer said, are still implementing Mr. Trump's directive, so the states are not harmed by "hypothetical future actions."

The executive order "functions as an internal directive from the President to subordinate officials and agencies to engage in future policymaking," he wrote. "Respondents' real concern is not with the Order itself — which does not require anyone outside the government to do (or refrain from doing) anything — but with possible harms that may arise depending upon what specific actions the agencies ultimately decide to take in implementing the President's directives."

Sauer argued that it is the government that is harmed by the district court's injunction, especially with mail voting starting in some states in just weeks.

"Every day that the district court's injunction remains in place, it blocks the government's ability to finalize and implement the President's proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November," he wrote.

In response to the administration's request, the Democratic-led states warned that allowing the president's executive order would lead to confusion and risks disenfranchising millions of voters who rely on mail ballots.

Granting the administration emergency relief "would allow the federal government to rush out an unprecedented, legally indefensible voter-verification and ballot-interception program that would, among other things, give the U.S. Postal Service far-reaching new powers and responsibilities," the state attorneys general wrote in a filing.

They also argued that the states are harmed by the executive order because it forces them to take steps to comply with its policies for the upcoming November elections.

Without the injunction from the lower court, the state and local election administrators would be forced to divert time and resources away from election-preparation work "to compile and convert voluminous data for submission to USPS, train elections officials, educate voters, and change their ballot envelopes," the attorneys general said.

In addition to the 23 states, a coalition of Democratic campaign committees filed a lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's mail voting executive order. But in that dispute, filed in Washington, D.C., lower courts rebuffed Democrats' request to prevent the directive's implementation.

In an unsigned decision last month, a unanimous panel of three judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit said that the case is not yet ripe for review.

"If the defendant agencies take steps to implement the Executive Order in a manner that violates federal law or the Constitution, Plaintiffs can promptly seek relief," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

Mr. Trump has long criticized mail voting and asserted that significant numbers of noncitizens are voting in federal elections, though he has not provided evidence in support of that claim. It is illegal under federal law for noncitizens to cast ballots in U.S. elections, and instances of noncitizen voting are rare.

Still, with the midterm elections fast approaching, the president is pressing Congress to significantly curb mail voting and impose new requirements for voter registration. His administration has also overhauled a federal database maintained by DHS to verify citizenship and immigration status.

But a different federal judge blocked the administration's use of the centralized clearinghouse and found it had been used by some states to incorrectly remove U.S. citizens from their voter rolls.

Meanwhile, the Justice Department has sued dozens of states to obtain their voter rolls, though judges have rebuffed those efforts.
