The United Kingdom was the first country to donate long-range strike weapons to Kyiv, in 2023.

British Defence Minister Luke Pollard told the BBC the release of information was intended to allow Ukraine to defend itself. He said Russian strikes were also hitting shopping centres and housing. Zelensky has requested 360 Patriot interceptor missiles, supplies of which from the United States have been reduced by the conflict with Iran.

The visit follows accusations by Russia's embassy in London that the United Kingdom had deliberately opted for escalation, after the use of British drones in strikes inside Russia came to light, with a warning that the deeper Britain's involvement, the higher the price it would pay. Moscow also confirmed that its ambassador in London, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in recent weeks with no successor named. The Russian mission told the BBC this did not reflect an intention to downgrade bilateral relations.

Exchanges of attacks continued overnight. Russian local authorities reported two children killed and seven injured by debris from a Ukrainian drone that struck a private children's centre, and a fire at a warehouse belonging to the retailer Ozon, the third in three days. Kharkiv governor Oleh Syniehubov reported three people killed in a Russian attack. None of the tolls can be independently verified.

World.title: Isaac del Toro wins his first Tour of Germany
World.content:
Mexican cyclist Isaac del Toro once again put Mexico at the forefront of international cycling after winning the 40th Deutschland Tour (Tour of Germany), one of the most prestigious stage races on the European calendar.

At 22 years old, this victory makes Del Toro the first Latin American cyclist to win the Tour of Germany, following his recent milestone of becoming the first Mexican cyclist in 36 years to win a stage of the Tour de France.

😱 75 Meter fehlen 🇲🇽 Isaac del Toro zum zweiten Etappensieg! 🇫🇷 Paul Magnier gewinnt in Heilbronn vor 🇳🇱 Danny van Poppel und 🇩🇪 Tim Torn Teutenberg. 👕 Isaac del Toro ist der Gesamtsieger der 🇩🇪 #DeineTour 2026! 🏆#DeutschlandTour pic.twitter.com/8iWFYttYv1 — Tour de France – DE (@letour_de) August 23, 2026

The star cyclist finished the four-stage race with an accumulated time of 17 hours, 39 minutes and 48 seconds, while Frenchman Louis Barré finished second, 53 seconds behind. Swiss rider Marc Hirschi completed the podium, 1:08 back.

Sunday’s final stage covered 156.5 kilometers around Heilbronn, with a route marked by constant climbs and descents.

With the German championship, Del Toro, originally from Ensenada, secured his twentieth professional title since winning his first in 2013 at the Tour de l’Avenir. In 2016, he also won the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico and Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes.

The Tour of Germany, which ran from Aug. 19 to Aug. 23, also saw the participation of Edgar “Chucky” Cadena, 26, originally from Mexico City.

Chucky was Mexico’s national champion before Del Toro, and is part of a broader generation of athletes working to bring Mexican cyclists back to major competitions.

Participating in Team Storck-MRW Bau, Chucky tried to surprise with an attack 1.5 kilometers from the finish line. With a steady pace in the mountain stages, Chucky’s stamina on the toughest climbs allowed him to quietly climb the standings, securing the No. 10 spot overall.

With reports from Infobae and ESPN

World.title: University of Guadalajara scientists discover 6 ant-killing ‘zombie fungi’
World.content:
Six newly documented species of “zombie fungi” — parasites that hijack the behavior of ants and drive them to their deaths — have been identified in western Jalisco, marking the first scientific record in Mexico of the unusual fungus.

One of the new described species, Ophiocordyceps deltoroi, was named for Guadalajara-born filmmaker Guillermo del Toro, whose work often blends horror and fantasy.

Researchers from the University of Guadalajara (UdeG) found the fungi in a tropical forest near the Haravéri Botanical Garden in San Sebastián del Oeste, Jalisco.

Their study was published online late last year, then drew wider attention this month after reports highlighted the species named for Del Toro.

The six species belong to the Ophiocordyceps unilateralis complex, a group of ant-parasitizing fungi found in tropical forests worldwide.

After infecting an ant by penetrating its outer cuticle, the fungi produce metabolites that alter the ant’s behavior.

The infected ants ultimately clamp their mandibles onto tree bark, leaves or rocks in the forest. After the ant dies, the fungus grows from its body and releases spores, helping infect new hosts.

“It’s both monstrous and beautiful at the same time,” César Ballesteros Aguirre, the UdeG mycologist who led the work, said in a university news release.

The discovery is the first scientific record in Mexico of the so-called “zombie-ant fungi,” according to the university. The team is also studying fungi near metropolitan Guadalajara and parasites of butterflies and wasps.

The fungi are not known to pose a threat to people. Their highly specialized relationships with insect hosts differ sharply from portrayals such as “The Last of Us,” a fictional HBO series in which a mutated Cordyceps fungus spreads to humans and turns them into violent, zombie-like creatures.

Beyond the taxonomy, the UdeG work establishes a baseline for studying Mexico’s fungal biodiversity, the parasites’ relationships with their ant hosts and the chemical compounds they produce.

Their discovery provides a starting point for researchers to catalog the fungi’s metabolites and test them for biological activity.

Some related insect-pathogenic fungi have produced compounds of interest to researchers studying potential biomedical applications and pest control.

However, the new Jalisco species have not been shown to treat any disease, and any potential scientific applications would require substantially more study.

With reports from TV Azteca, Tribuna de México and Infobae

World.title: Mexico’s economy grew 1.4% in Q2 but contracted in June, revised data shows
World.content:
Listen to this article

The Mexican economy grew 1.4% on a quarter-over-quarter basis between April and June and 1.9% in annual terms, according to revised data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Monday.

Both growth rates were slightly lower than those reported by INEGI in preliminary data published July 30.

However, they still represent a significant improvement from the 0.3% sequential contraction and modest annual growth the Mexican economy registered in the first quarter of 2026. The 1.4% quarter-over-quarter growth between April and June was the best second-quarter result since 2021.

Analysts partially attributed the solid performance in the second quarter to spending related to the FIFA men’s World Cup, which Mexico co-hosted with the United States and Canada in June and July.

INEGI also reported on Monday that the Mexican economy grew 1.2% annually in the first six months of 2026.

Primary sector records strongest Q2 growth

INEGI’s final data shows that Mexico’s primary sector — which includes economic activities related to agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting — expanded 2.4% in the second quarter compared to the first three months of the year. In annual terms, the primary sector grew 4.8%.

The secondary and tertiary sectors also grew in sequential and annual terms in the second quarter, but their expansions were more modest.

The secondary sector — which includes manufacturing, construction and mining as well as electricity, gas and water-related activities — grew 1.6% on a quarter-over-quarter basis and 0.9% annually.

The tertiary, or services, sector grew 1.4% compared to the first quarter of 2026 and 2.3% in annual terms.

INEGI reports a month-over-month contraction in June — and an uptick in inflation

INEGI on Monday also published final economic growth data for June and inflation data for the first half of August.

Mexico’s economy contracted 0.1% in June compared to May and grew 1.7% in annual terms. It was the second consecutive month-over-month decline after a 0.4% contraction in May. The construction sector was a standout performer in June, growing 3% compared to May and 4.2% in annual terms.

INEGI data also showed that Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate rose to 3.26% in the first 15 days of August, up from 3.12% across July.

In the first half of August, Mexico’s annual core inflation rate, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was 3.93%, down slightly from a 3.95% reading in July.

The outlook for the Mexican economy

Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote on X on Monday that her estimate, based on the latest GDP data and the growth of the construction sector in June, was that the Mexican economy will grow 1.4% in 2026.

“Weakness in the consumption of domestic goods and services persists, so it’s still probable that a [sequential] contraction will be recorded in the third quarter,” she wrote.

The Bank of Mexico is forecasting a 1.1% economic expansion this year, while the International Monetary Fund anticipates that the Mexican economy will grow 1.2%. The federal Finance Ministry is more optimistic, forecasting economic growth in the range of 1.8%-2.8% in 2026.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Another major bust nets weapons, drugs and 20 CJNG-related arrests
World.content:
Federal authorities dismantled a major criminal cell over the weekend, arresting 20 people and seizing weapons and exotic animals.

The joint operation targeted a network allegedly linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and featured simultaneous raids on 36 properties in the states of Hidalgo, Jalisco and Michoacán.

In an official statement, Mexico’s Security Ministry said the Aug. 21-23 operation was the result of intelligence and investigative work by the Defense Ministry, the Navy, the Security Ministry, the Federal Attorney General’s Office and the National Guard.

The statement said that the operation resulted “in the arrest of 20 individuals linked to the CJNG,” adding that “authorities seized 10 firearms (seven handguns and three rifles), drugs, 113 vehicles, tigers, panthers, as well as other animals and birds kept in inadequate conditions.”

Officials also confiscated cash and jewelry, communications equipment, a drone and a drone jammer, while specifying that in addition to the firearms seized, agents gathered up magazines and cartridges of various calibers. The drugs confiscated were said to be unspecified doses of fentanyl and methamphetamine, as well as marijuana.

The Defense Ministry said the 20 detainees were transferred in a Mexican Navy aircraft and placed at the disposal of the Attorney General’s Office (FGR) in Mexico City “to continue with the corresponding investigations and expert analyses to determine their legal status.”

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the goal of these operations is not only “to stop those who generate violence, but to steadily weaken the operational, logistical and financial capabilities of criminal organizations.”

García Harfuch said the authorities will “continue with coordinated intelligence, investigation and territorial presence efforts” to protect and defend the public interest.

The outcome of this latest tactical operation brings to 32 the total number of alleged CJNG members apprehended by security forces in less than a week.

On Aug. 19, the Army led a major security operation in Michoacán targeting CJNG leader Heraclio Guerrero Martínez, alias “El Tío Lako.” The 15-hour raid resulted in nine to 12 arrests — including the target’s partner and daughter.

With reports from Excelsior, Milenio and Aristegui Noticias

World.title: Why Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya returned to office for only 48 hours
World.content:
Rubén Rocha Moya, the Sinaloa governor who is accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors, returned to office on Friday — only to ask to go on leave again the very next day.

The 77-year-old governor’s submission of a request to take indefinite leave came after representatives of his own party — Morena — rejected his decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa almost four months after he first left office. The Sinaloa Congress approved his leave request on Sunday.

In a social media post on Saturday, President Claudia Sheinbaum also indicated that she didn’t agree with Rocha’s decision to return to office. The president — the leader of the “fourth transformation” (4T) movement with which Rocha is also affiliated — explicitly expressed that position on Monday.

Rocha, who became governor of Sinaloa in late 2021, first decided to take leave in early May shortly after the unsealing of a U.S. indictment accusing him and nine other current and former Sinaloa-based officials of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

The U.S. Justice Department said on April 29 that the governor allegedly attended meetings with “the Chapitos” — sons of convicted drug trafficker Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán — and allowed the Sinaloa Cartel faction they lead to “operate with impunity in Sinaloa.”

Rocha, who is also accused of weapons offenses, promptly rejected the accusations against him. To date, he has avoided extradition to the United States as — according to the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) in Mexico — U.S. authorities have not presented sufficient evidence against him. Sheinbaum has endorsed the FGR’s view and stressed that Mexican legal processes and sovereignty must be respected. However, now, more than ever, she is seeking to distance herself and her government from Rocha, whose indictment has raised serious and broader questions about alleged corruption and alleged collusion between Morena and organized crime.

The governor’s decision to return to office on Friday surprised — and in some cases outraged — millions of Mexicans, including members of the federal government. His brief return to office restored his constitutional immunity from prosecution, according to experts, but he presumably lost that immunity (called fuero in Mexico) by going on leave once again.

Here is a timeline of relevant events between Friday. Aug. 21 and Monday, Aug. 24.

Friday morning: Rocha announces his return to office

In a social media post shortly before 10 a.m. on Friday, Rocha announced that he had resumed his position as governor of Sinaloa.

“It is my duty to fulfill the mandate of the people of Sinaloa, who elected me as head of the executive branch to govern until October 31, 2027,” he wrote.

“During the period of my temporary leave from office, which I requested from the State Congress on May 1 of this year, I placed myself at the disposal of our country’s justice system in order to be investigated regarding the false accusations … that a U.S. government office leveled against me without any evidence, seeking to undermine our national sovereignty through its statements and slander,” Rocha wrote.

The governor wrote that he had personally appeared before the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) during his leave of absence. That institute, he said, determined that there was no evidence against him.

“In other words, I haven’t committed any crime,” Rocha wrote.

“… Today I return to fulfilling my duties as Governor of Sinaloa with a clear conscience, with my head held high, and with the power of the truth on our side.”

Early Friday afternoon: SEGOB says that Rocha’s decision to return to office was a ‘personal’ one

In a statement issued early Friday afternoon, the federal Interior Ministry (SEGOB) sought to distance the federal government from Rocha’s decision to return to office.

“The Interior Ministry reports that the decision of Dr. Rubén Rocha Moya to resume his duties as governor of the state of Sinaloa is exclusively a determination of a personal nature,” SEGOB said.

The ministry noted that the FGR opened investigations into the 10 people accused of drug trafficking and weapons offenses by U.S. prosecutors, among whom is Rocha, a Morena senator and the mayor of Culiacán.

SEGOB highlighted that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has asked the U.S. Department of Justice on repeated occasions to “provide the evidence that supports the accusations.”

“In that sense, it is up to the Federal Attorney General’s Office, within the domain of its powers and in accordance with the advance of the investigations, to provide additional information it considers pertinent,” the Interior Ministry said.

Late Friday afternoon: Morena lawmakers speak out

Later on Friday afternoon, Morena deputies expressed their opposition to Rocha’s decision to return to office.

In a statement, Morena deputies called on the governor to “reconsider his decision” so that the FGR and “other authorities” can continue and conclude their investigations “with full autonomy.”

Comunicado del Grupo Parlamentario de Morena pic.twitter.com/5S3wYRYkB7 — Arturo Ávila. (@arturoavila_mx) August 22, 2026

Morena senators echoed SEGOB’s sentiment, saying in a statement that Rocha’s decision to return to office was a “personal and individual action.”

Friday evening: Morena governors weigh in

The Morena governors of 22 states as well as Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada and the Green Party governor of San Luis Potosí released a statement on Friday evening expressing their opposition to Rocha’s return to office in Sinaloa.

“In the fourth transformation, individual decisions will never be above the collective project or the citizens’ mandate,” said the 4T political leaders.

“… No authority is empowered to act at the margin of the law or to take unilateral decisions that threaten constitutional order or republican dialogue,” they said.

“Personal or group political projects have no place when they counteract the well-being of the nation. We call on Dr. Rubén Rocha Moya to act with maturity and responsibility,” said the 23 governors and Brugada.

“Politics is an exercise of congruence. Excess and factional decisions go against principles of honesty and loyalty that we swore to uphold.”

Saturday morning: Sheinbaum enters the fray

In a social media post on Friday morning, Sheinbaum announced that she was sick with the flu and therefore didn’t perform any public duties that day, and didn’t comment on Rocha’s return to office.

The president returned to social media on Saturday morning to publish a message that was clearly aimed at Rocha, although she didn’t mention the governor by name.

“No personal interest can ever be above the interests of the people and the nation,” she wrote.

“And certainly not when what is being placed above Mexico is not the well-being of its people, but the naked ambition of power for power’s sake,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Power without principles becomes arrogance; power without limits becomes abuse; and power that forgets the people ultimately finds itself at odds with history,” she wrote.

Ningún interés personal puede estar jamás por encima de los intereses del pueblo y de la Nación. Y mucho menos cuando aquello que se pretende colocar por encima de México no es el bienestar de su gente, sino la ambición desnuda del poder por el poder.

Porque el poder sin… — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 22, 2026

“Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but the responsibility to the nation is eternal. The people are not here to feed personal ambitions: they are here to demand that their dignity, their future, and their hope be defended. Above any name, any group, and any personal interest stand the people and the nation.”

In a separate social media post on Saturday morning, the director of the Sinaloa-based Noroeste newspaper, Adrían López Ortiz, wrote:

“I see many outsiders saying that Sinaloenses are speaking out against Rocha. I’ll give you a fact. Yesterday, @noroestemx tried to ask people in the center of Culiacán what they thought about his return [but] they were scared to respond on camera.”

Sinaloa is a violence-plagued state where the Los Chapitos and Los Mayos factions of the Sinaloa Cartel are engaged in a long-running and extremely bloody civil war. Cartel violence has ravaged the Sinaloa economy and led many residents to take extra safety precautions, such as limiting their movements at night.

Saturday evening: Rocha heeds Sheinbaum’s words

In a social media post on Saturday evening, Rocha published a letter addressed to the president of the Sinaloa Congress in which he requested “temporary leave” of an “indefinite nature” from his job as governor.

Above the letter, he wrote: “Sinaloa, the nation and the transformation movement are above everything.”

Sunday morning: Sinaloa Congress approves Rocha’s leave request

In an extraordinary session on Sunday morning, Sinaloa state lawmakers unanimously approved Rocha’s request to go on indefinite leave.

Monday morning: Sheinbaum says Rocha’s decision to return to office was ‘imprudent’

At her Monday morning press conference, Sheinbaum said that she found out about Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa via his social media post on Friday.

“I didn’t have any prior knowledge that he wanted to return to his duties in the state of Sinaloa,” she said.

“The truth is that I didn’t think it was appropriate, to say the least,” Sheinbaum said.

Later in the press conference, the president explicitly said she didn’t agree with Rocha’s decision to return to the governorship of Sinaloa.

“At the very least, I thought it was imprudent,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Nothing personal can be above the interests of the people of Sinaloa and the people of Mexico,” she said.

Sheinbaum said on Sunday that Rocha’s decision to once again leave the governorship was “the best thing for Sinaloa.”

On Monday, she noted that the Sinaloa Congress has to appoint an interim governor until a new governor takes office in late 2027 following the Sinaloa gubernatorial election in June of next year. She said that the interim governor should be a person who is honest, professional and dedicated to “the people of Sinaloa.”

Sheinbaum subsequently described claims that former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador told Rocha to return to the governorship of Sinaloa as “political fiction.”

World.title: MND Local: Flight cuts and water relief in Guadalajara, and Jalisco’s tequila economy
World.content:
This week brings another round of international flight schedule changes at Guadalajara International Airport. Also in this week’s update, the government clarifies who is eligible for 80% discounts from SIAPA due to poor-quality tap water, plus an update on Jalisco’s tequila economy.

Aeroméxico suspends flights from Guadalajara to Northern California, Chicago

Last week, Aeroméxico suspended several important routes between Guadalajara and the U.S., including nonstop flights to San Francisco, Sacramento, Fresno and Chicago, according to schedule filings tracked by AeroRoutes.

The route suspensions are in effect from now until mid-December, with no clarity on whether they might resume after that.

Aeroméxico’s suspended routes and dates in effect

Route Dates of suspension Guadalajara to Chicago (ORD) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to San Francisco (SFO) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to Fresno (FAT) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026 Guadalajara to Sacramento (SMF) Aug. 17, 2026 – Dec. 16, 2026

Under Aeroméxico’s disruption rules, ticketed customers on canceled routes are entitled to a route and schedule change or a refund. Before calling the airline to request rebooking, it is a good idea to confirm that your itinerary is no longer available on its website.

It is also wise to keep any receipts for hotels, ground transport and nonrefundable side bookings tied to your original Aeroméxico itinerary. Those costs can influence whether the airline grants a reissue, refund or full cancellation of the original ticket.

Competing carriers such as United Airlines and the ultra-low-cost carriers Volaris and Viva Aerobus still service these cities to and from Guadalajara, so travelers have a few alternatives left that eliminate the need to connect in Mexico City.

Who is eligible for 80% discounts from SIAPA due to poor water quality?

A hot topic in Guadalajara lately has been the question of who is — and is not — eligible for a discount on their water bill from SIAPA (the Intermunicipal Water and Sewerage Services System in Jalisco) stemming from chronic water quality issues in the Guadalajara metropolitan area.

After weeks of speculation, we finally have some answers.

As of Aug. 17, an 80% discount will be applied to water bills in 203 neighborhoods in Guadalajara, Zapopan, Tlaquepaque and Tonalá affected by serious water quality problems. The initiative aims to compensate users who have reported various problems with water coming from their taps, including foul-smelling, dirty or discolored water.

The Jalisco Congress formalized the benefit, and the SIAPA Governing Board approved the first list of beneficiary neighborhoods, with details published on Aug. 14 in the Official Gazette of Jalisco.

Popular expatriate neighborhoods such as Ladrón de Guevara, Santa Teresita and Providencia in Guadalajara, as well as Chapalita and Seattle in Zapopan, are all eligible for the discount. To see the full list of neighborhoods, check Annex A of this document.

How to claim the SIAPA discount

Economic relief is aimed at residential users and small businesses in the designated neighborhoods who consume up to 25 cubic meters of water per month. Those who consume more than this amount are ineligible.

To qualify, households and businesses must also demonstrate that they are up to date on all of their payments to SIAPA to receive the discount. In other words, those who stopped paying for contaminated water out of frustration and are still in arrears cannot obtain a discount.

There are also 32 neighborhoods still under review for eligibility, so if your neighborhood is not on the current list, it may still be added later as SIAPA makes adjustments.

Residents can access the discount until Dec. 15, 2026.

Tequila exports showed signs of recovery in the first half of 2026

Despite the trade uncertainty surrounding negotiations of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), the tequila business appears to be resurgent in 2026, following sluggish results in 2025.

According to figures from the Tequila Regulatory Council (CRT), total tequila exports during the first half of this year reached 215 million liters, up 3.4% from the 208 million liters exported abroad in the same period of 2025. The U.S. remains the largest export market for Mexican tequila by far (taking roughly 81% of the total).

Following a period of explosive growth in demand from 2020 to 2024 where growth averaged 8.5% per year, demand for Jalisco’s most famous beverage has leveled off. The slowdown stems mainly from reduced demand for super-premium tequila in the U.S., as consumers traded down or explored sobriety following the coronavirus pandemic’s well-documented drinking binge.

In response, Jalisco’s producers have been working to correct an agave oversupply problem (too many fields were planted during boom times) and develop new business in Europe, Latin America and Asia to reduce their dependence on the U.S. consumer.

Based on the trend year to date, the Tequila Regulatory Council is cautiously optimistic for better times ahead for the state’s 229 authorized producers and more than 3,400 registered brands.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Profepa clears 6 dolphins for relocation from shuttered Cancún dolphinarium
World.content:
Six of the nine dolphins living at the now-shuttered Dolphin Discovery installations, located within the former Ventura Park in Cancún, Quintana Roo, are considered candidates to begin a preparation process for a possible relocation, according to a report by the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa).

The move comes amid concerns about the health and safety of the animals, which remain under the care of Mexico’s environmental authority following the closure of the dolphinarium in October last year after videos surfaced of the dolphins displaying extreme distress.

Profepa stated that the nine dolphins – two females and seven males – are in delicate clinical condition, meaning their transfer cannot be immediate and each animal will require an individual protocol.

Since May, Profepa has been working to medically stabilize the dolphins through veterinary checkups, laboratory tests and monitoring of their behavior, feeding and response to treatment, the agency told Mongabay.

However, activist groups in defense of animal rights, including Veeleaf and Tide Breakers, have shared images and videos criticizing the care of the nine dolphins that remain in captivity. Reportedly, the dolphins are in small pools where they can barely move, are fed smaller portions of food than required and spend all their time in the sun, with no shade.

The future of these dolphins is tied to a reform that sought to transform the operations of dolphinariums in Mexico.

In July 2025, the Mexican Senate unanimously approved a nationwide ban on dolphin and other marine mammal shows, as well as the breeding of marine mammals in captivity except for conservation purposes.

The new regulations mandate the transfer of cetaceans to marine pens, or fenced-off ocean enclosures that slowly reintroduce the dolphins to their natural habitat, and limit interactions with those already under human care, prohibiting practices that could compromise their well-being.

However, the regulations needed to establish the application criteria have not been published yet; hence, the nine dolphins remain in the same pools where they have spent a good part of their lives.

The organization Empty the Tanks is demanding that the dolphins be temporarily transferred to existing marine pools at the Dolphin Discovery facilities in Isla Mujeres and Chankanaab, Cozumel. “We are not asking that they be released into the ocean. We are asking for a responsible, feasible measure backed by scientific evidence: that they be allowed to live in a much more natural environment while receiving the care they need,” the organization said in a statement.

According to a statement by Profepa, “All the decisions that have been made aim to ensure the best possible well-being of the dolphins, to help them survive in the best way possible and to alleviate their suffering.”

“We know that moving them to a semi-open enclosure at sea would be an improvement, but first we must guarantee that this move does not cost them their lives,” the statement continues.

With reports from Infobae, Por Esto! and Reportur

World.title: Aura farming battles make their debut in Mexico
World.content:
With a nod to the “You got served” hip-hop dance battle craze of two decades ago, kids and young adults in Mexico have begun to stage “aura farming” battles in public squares across the country.

What the heck is aura farming, you ask? Fair question …

Aura farming is a viral internet slang trend that describes doing intentional, effortless things to look confident or charismatic. Gen Alpha and Gen Z use the term to describe doing something to improve your “vibe,” your style or your perceived social status, without seeming like you’re trying too hard.

It even warrants a definition in Merriam-Webster: “the act of doing something to look cool, impressive, stylish, etc., especially — and importantly — without trying too hard.”

The concept grew on TikTok and Instagram, combining the video game concept of “farming” (carrying out repetitive actions for points), before dancing was attached to it, eventually evolving into physical “aura battles” in parks and streets across Latin America.

In Mexico City, three notorious aura farming battles took place last week: on Friday at the esplanade of the Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City; on Saturday at the Monument to the Revolution; and on Sunday in the Condesa neighborhood (where there was even a prize of 3,000 pesos, or US $177).

The craze has reached beyond the capital, too.

Aura battles have recently been staged in Juárez Park in Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz, and children as young as six years old participated in a competition in Torreón, Coahuila.

Compiten en Concurso para "Farmear Aura" en Veracruz

Watch this video on YouTube

The “battles” attract massive crowds who watch participants compete symbolically with poses, dances, gestures and meme references to demonstrate who has more “aura.”

A winner is determined by crowd reaction (the volume of cheers, applause, laughter) and by the general impact made during the face-off. Essentially, the social presence displayed is “scored” like an imaginary video game.

Unfortunately, the events also have their detractors. The municipal council of Ignacio de la Llave, Veracruz, officially prohibited aura battles in public parks, arguing that it was not due to the theme or content of the competition, but rather “a strict matter of administrative procedures and regulations for public spaces.”

CNN traces the origin of aura farming to 2024 and said it gained international attention last year through viral videos of 11-year-old Indonesian Rayyan Arkan Dikha dancing at the front of a boat in a traditional rowing competition. Social media users commented on the high levels of “aura” the boy possessed and it took off from there.

The trend has become particularly popular in Latin America: A “championship” was staged at the University of Costa Rica in San Juan on Aug. 18 and several tournaments were organized in São Paulo, Brazil, this summer.

With reports from CNN, LatinUS, Infobae and Telediario

World.title: Paraguay Investment Approvals Hit US$448 Million, Up 32%
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Paraguay · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Paraguay’s industry ministry approved US$448 million in investments across 116 projects in seven months.

— How big The approved total grew 32% compared with the same period last year.

— The catch These are approved project amounts, not yet disbursed to companies or spent.

The Quintet Brings Tango Legacy

This ensemble is the official group founded by Piazzolla himself. It now tours internationally to keep his revolutionary music alive.

The ‘Le Grand Tango’ tour is named after one of Piazzolla’s most famous compositions. That piece, originally written for cello and piano, showcases his dramatic style.

Colombian audiences will hear the quintet’s signature sound, which includes bandoneon, violin, piano, bass, and guitar. Each concert promises a deep dive into Piazzolla’s rich repertoire.

Tour Dates Across Four Cities

Astor Piazzolla was born in 1921 in Argentina and grew up in New York. He learned the bandoneon as a child and later studied with the famous composer Nadia Boulanger.

Piazzolla revolutionized tango in the 1950s by creating nuevo tango, a style that added complex harmonies and improvisation. This innovation drew both praise and criticism from traditionalists.

His music combined the passion of tango with the structure of classical music and the freedom of jazz. Pieces like ‘Libertango’ and ‘Adios Nonino’ became worldwide classics.

Piazzolla died in 1992, but his legacy lives on through the quintet that bears his name. The ensemble preserves his original arrangements and continues to perform them for new generations.

— How big The regime covers people with active lawsuits seeking payment from the state for certain public programs, pending final judgment.

— The catch The reform does not guarantee payment to all claimants and does not alter final court judgments already in force.

— Who pays The Ministry of Finance (Sefin) may identify and allocate funds for these obligations, subject to budget availability.

— What comes next Validated agreements must be formalized within 45 business days and paid within no more than 18 months.

— What is unknown Initial reports did not disclose the vote count or the names of the reform’s sponsors or legislators.

The National Congress approved a reform creating a temporary conciliation regime for active payment lawsuits against the state, pending budget availability.

Honduras’s National Congress approved the reform on 24 August 2026, creating a temporary conciliation regime for lawsuits against the state. Claimants can now negotiate payment agreements before their case ends, but approval depends on proving their claim and available budget.

Tegucigalpa; Honduras is advancing reforms meant to curb lawsuits against the state.

What the Reform Changes

Honduras’s National Congress approved a reform to the Law for Economic Reactivation and Human Development on 24 August 2026. The reform creates a temporary, special conciliation regime for people with active lawsuits against the state.

This regime applies to lawsuits against the state seeking payment tied to certain public programs. Claimants can now request conciliation while their lawsuit is still pending, instead of waiting for a final judgment.

The change offers a new path for resolving payment disputes before cases fully end in court. It does not automatically pay everyone with lawsuits against the state, as reported by Infobae on 24 August 2026.

The regime is temporary and special, designed for a specific window of opportunity. It focuses on active lawsuits, meaning cases that have not yet received a final ruling.

Who Qualifies for the Regime

To qualify, claimants must prove three essential things about their case. First, they must show they actually provided the service they claim payment for.

Second, they must demonstrate they have not been paid for that service. Third, the case must still be active without a final ruling from a court.

This means the regime applies only to pending disputes, not to cases already decided. Claimants with final judgments in force are not covered by this temporary conciliation path.

The verification process ensures the state can confirm the validity of each claim in lawsuits against the state. It also helps determine which claims are eligible for negotiation and potential payment.

How Agreements Will Be Formalized

Once a claim is validated and budget is available, the agreement must be formalized within 45 business days. This timeline is a key requirement of the new reform.

Payment under the agreement must be completed within no more than 18 months from formalization. This sets a clear deadline for the state to fulfill its obligations.

The Ministry of Finance, known as Sefin, may identify and allocate funds specifically for these obligations. This gives the finance ministry a central role in the process.

Budget availability is a critical condition for formalizing any agreement. Without available funds, claimants may not secure a payment deal even if their claim is valid.

The Role of the Finance Ministry

Sefin, the Ministry of Finance, is tasked with identifying and allocating funds for these payment obligations. This means the ministry must find money within the state budget to cover validated claims.

The reform does not guarantee payment to all claimants, as approval depends on budget availability. The finance ministry’s ability to allocate funds is a determining factor for each agreement.

This arrangement gives Sefin significant discretion in deciding which claims can be paid. The ministry must balance these obligations with other state spending priorities.

The process allows the state to negotiate the amount and payment terms for each claim. Some claimants may receive less or different payment conditions than they originally sought in court.

Limits of the Conciliation Regime

The reform does not guarantee payment to everyone who has sued the state over unpaid services. It creates a pathway for negotiation, but approval depends on proof and budget.

The regime is limited to pending cases and does not alter final court judgments already in force. This means cases with existing rulings are not affected by the reform.

Because the state must verify each claim and can negotiate terms, outcomes vary among claimants. Some may receive less than their original court demand or different payment conditions.

The temporary nature of the regime adds urgency for eligible claimants to request conciliation. Once the period ends, the option may no longer be available for new requests.

Reporting on the Congressional Approval

Infobae reported on 24 August 2026 that the Congress approved the reform on that Thursday. El Reportero HN Radio also published details on 20 August 2026 about the same reform.

The available reports describe the approval by the National Congress but do not name a specific sponsor or legislator behind the reform. The vote tally also has not been disclosed in initial reporting.

This lack of detail means the public does not know who championed the reform or how it was passed. It also leaves open questions about the level of support in Congress.

The reports focus on the practical changes for claimants rather than the political process. They highlight the conciliation regime and its requirements for eligible lawsuits.

Implications for Claimants

For individuals with active lawsuits against the state, the reform offers a new opportunity to resolve payment disputes. They can now request conciliation and potentially reach an agreement without waiting for a final court ruling.

Claimants must act quickly to prove their case meets all three requirements. They need to show they provided the service, were not paid, and that their case remains open.

The outcome depends on budget availability, which the finance ministry controls. Claimants may need to accept negotiated amounts that differ from their original demands.

The reform does not change the legal status of their lawsuit, as it remains pending until an agreement is reached. If no agreement is formalized, the case continues through the normal court process.

What Comes Next

The next step is for eligible claimants to request conciliation under the new regime. The state and claimants will then enter negotiations to determine payment terms.

The finance ministry must identify and allocate funds for these obligations. This will be a critical test of whether the reform leads to actual payments.

Concerns remain that the reform does not guarantee payment and may result in different terms than original claims. The temporary regime offers hope but not certainty for most claimants.

Initial reports did not disclose the vote count or sponsor names, leaving gaps in public understanding. Observers will watch how the regime is implemented and whether it resolves disputes effectively.

Frequently Asked Questions

No, the reform is limited to pending cases and does not alter final court judgments already in force. Who manages the funds for these payments? The Ministry of Finance, known as Sefin, may identify and allocate funds for these obligations. Budget availability is a key condition for each agreement.

World.content:

Costa Rica · SOCIETY

Key Facts — What happened Two Costa Rica earthquakes struck the Coronado area early Monday, causing minor local damage.

— How big The first quake measured M5.4 per RSN, with aftershock M4.8 about two minutes later.

— The catch Different agencies reported conflicting magnitudes for the first quake, from M4.9 to M5.4.

— Who pays Local residents face repair costs, while the National Emergency Commission (CNE) manages response.

— What comes next Monitoring continues as more than 30 aftershocks were recorded following the initial pair.

— Tsunami risk No tsunami warning was issued because these Costa Rica earthquakes struck inland, not offshore.

A pair of quakes rattled central Costa Rica before dawn, leaving only minor damage despite more than 30 aftershocks.

Two Costa Rica earthquakes hit the Coronado area early Monday 24 August 2026, with the first striking at 1:37 a.m. local time. Authorities confirmed no deaths or injuries, though minor damage was reported across several neighborhoods.

Two Costa Rica Earthquakes Shake Coronado Area, No Injuries. (Photo internet reproduction)

The sequence of events early Monday

Two Costa Rica earthquakes jolted the Coronado area before dawn on 24 August 2026. The first tremor hit at 1:37 a.m. local time, followed by a second about two minutes later.

The Red Sismológica Nacional (RSN) reported the first quake as M5.4 at a depth of 7 kilometers. Its epicenter was located 11 kilometers north of Cascajal, Vázquez de Coronado.

The second quake measured M4.8 at a depth of 10 kilometers, according to RSN. Both tremors occurred in the same general area of central Costa Rica.

Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks after the initial pair of quakes. Residents reported feeling several strong shakes throughout the early morning hours.

How different agencies measured the first quake

The three main monitoring institutions gave different magnitudes for the first tremor. The RSN revised its reading to M5.4, while the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVSICORI) initially reported M5.0.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) listed the event as M4.9 near the town of Cot at a depth of 10 kilometers. OVSICORI placed its epicenter near San Isidro de Coronado at 11 kilometers depth.

These discrepancies are common because agencies process preliminary data differently. The RSN later revised its reading, which is considered the most consistent final local value.

All agencies agreed the quake was shallow, between 7 and 11 kilometers deep. Such shallow depth typically increases shaking intensity near the epicenter.

Damage reports from affected communities

Damage from these Costa Rica earthquakes was minor and localized, according to emergency officials. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) reported only isolated incidents across the affected region.

A damaged house wall was reported in Dulce Nombre de Jesús, a community near the epicenter. A fallen utility pole was confirmed in San Vicente de Moravia, disrupting local power briefly.

Debris on Route 32 near kilometre 30 caused traffic delays for early commuters. Road crews cleared the material quickly, restoring normal flow within hours.

No deaths or injuries were confirmed by any agency following the earthquake sequence. The relatively minor damage reflects the moderate size of these tremors.

Why no tsunami warning was issued

No tsunami warning was issued for these Costa Rica earthquakes, and none was expected. Both quakes struck inland, not beneath the ocean floor where tsunamis can form.

The United States Tsunami Warning System explicitly stated no tsunami statement was issued for the event. This is standard procedure for earthquakes that occur on land.

Tsunami alerts are reserved for undersea quakes capable of displacing large water volumes. The Coronado area sits inland in the central highlands of Costa Rica.

Residents along the Pacific and Caribbean coasts experienced no unusual sea activity. The lack of an ocean connection made any tsunami threat virtually impossible.

Aftershock activity and ongoing monitoring

Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks following the main quakes on Monday morning. These smaller tremors continued for several hours after the initial pair.

Most aftershocks were too weak to be felt by residents, according to RSN. A few reached magnitudes that caused additional minor shaking in nearby communities.

The RSN and OVSICORI continue to monitor the seismic swarm closely. Both agencies are analyzing data from the sequence to understand the fault behavior.

Costa Rica sits in a seismically active region where such earthquake sequences are common. The country experiences hundreds of tremors each year, most too small to notice.

Public response and emergency coordination

The CNE activated its emergency protocols shortly after the first tremors were detected. Officials assessed damage across the Coronado area and surrounding districts.

Emergency crews inspected infrastructure including roads, bridges, and utility lines. They found only the fallen pole in Moravia and debris on Route 32.

Local authorities urged residents to remain calm and follow safety guidelines. Many people in San José and nearby cities felt the shaking and took precautions.

No evacuation orders were issued because damage levels did not warrant them. The response focused on quick damage assessment and restoring normal services.

Context of seismic activity in Costa Rica

Costa Rica Earthquakes are frequent because the country sits atop several active tectonic plate boundaries. The Cocos plate subducts beneath the Caribbean plate along the Pacific coast.

This collision zone generates frequent tremors of varying intensity across the country. The Coronado area has experienced earthquakes before due to local fault lines.

Scientists at OVSICORI and RSN continuously monitor these fault systems. Their early warning systems provide valuable seconds of notice before strong shaking arrives.

Monday’s pair of Costa Rica earthquakes was moderate compared to historic major events. The country’s building codes have improved significantly since destructive quakes in the past.

What residents should do after the quakes

Residents should check their homes for cracks in walls and damage to gas lines. The CNE recommends reporting any structural issues to local authorities promptly.

People should be prepared for possible continued aftershocks in coming days. Having an emergency kit with water, food, and flashlights is always advisable.

Those living near steep slopes should watch for landslides after heavy rain or shaking. Route 32 authorities will monitor the area for new debris falls.

Stay informed through official channels like CNE, RSN, and OVSICORI for updates. These Costa Rica earthquakes serve as a reminder to review personal emergency plans.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time did the two Costa Rica earthquakes occur on Monday? The first quake struck at 1:37 a.m. local time, followed by the second about two minutes later. Both tremors hit the Coronado area of central Costa Rica. How big were the earthquakes according to different agencies? The RSN measured the first quake at M5.4, while OVSICORI reported M5.0 and the USGS listed M4.9. The second quake was measured at M4.8 by RSN. Was there any damage from these earthquakes? Damage was minor: a damaged house wall in Dulce Nombre de Jesús and a fallen utility pole in San Vicente de Moravia. No injuries or deaths were confirmed. Was a tsunami warning issued after the quakes? No tsunami warning was issued because both earthquakes struck inland, not under the ocean. Such warnings are only necessary for undersea quakes that can displace water. How many aftershocks were recorded after the main quakes? Seismologists recorded more than 30 aftershocks following the initial pair of tremors. Most were weak but some caused additional minor shaking in nearby areas.

Central bank data shows steady expansion led by commerce, manufacturing and real estate.

Guatemala’s economic activity grew 4.4% in the first half of 2026, according to Banco de Guatemala (Banguat) data. The monthly activity index rose 4.2% year over year in June, up from 3.9% a year earlier.

Guatemala City’s National Palace; the economy grew 4.4% in the first half of 2026, the central bank says.

Central Bank Data Shows Solid Expansion

Guatemala growth reached 4.4% in the first six months of 2026, according to Banguat data reported on 21 and 22 August 2026. This accumulated figure measures economic activity through June, using the monthly IMAE indicator.

The IMAE, or monthly economic activity index, rose 4.2% year over year in June. This compares with a 3.9% increase in June 2025, showing slightly faster momentum.

Banguat, the central bank, compiles these statistics to track the country’s economic pulse. The June reading confirms a steady expansion in the first half of the year.

Economists watch the IMAE closely because it offers timely signals on economic health. The June data points to sustained growth across key sectors.

Commerce and Manufacturing Lead the Way

Commerce and vehicle repair activities were the main drivers of the IMAE growth in June. Manufacturing also contributed significantly to the monthly expansion.

Real estate activities added to the positive performance, according to the Banguat-based reporting. These three sectors together powered much of the 4.2% yearly rise.

Strong consumer demand helped fuel commerce, while manufacturing benefited from steady industrial output. Real estate activity reflected ongoing construction and property transactions.

The sector mix suggests broad-based growth rather than reliance on one area. This diversification supports the overall Guatemala growth narrative.

Banguat Raises Its GDP Forecast for 2026

Banguat raised its GDP forecast for 2026 in a separate outlook report, citing several supportive factors. The bank pointed to private consumption as a key engine of expansion.

Public and private investment are also expected to boost activity. Dynamic exports and remittances from abroad are helping support household spending, Banguat said.

Remittances, money sent home by Guatemalans working overseas, provide a steady income stream for many families. That supports consumption and overall demand.

The higher forecast reflects confidence in the economy’s momentum. This positive outlook aligns with the first-half growth data.

Private Consumption Drives Household Spending

Private consumption remains a critical pillar of the Guatemala growth story in 2026. Household spending is fueled by remittances and stable employment, according to Banguat.

Banguat’s analysis links the upswing directly to consumer demand. Public investment in infrastructure also plays a role in stimulating economic activity.

Private investment decisions by businesses add to the positive picture. Together, these factors create a supportive environment for sustained growth.

The central bank’s language suggests confidence in the durability of the current expansion. This stands out in a region with mixed economic performance.

Exports and Investment Bolster Economic Momentum

Dynamic exports are contributing to the economic upswing, Banguat reported on its 2026 outlook. External demand for Guatemalan goods adds to domestic strength.

Public and private investment together are helping build productive capacity. This investment supports job creation and long-term competitiveness.

The combination of exports and investment creates a balanced growth model. Banguat’s forecast revision reflects these positive trends.

Exports benefit from strong demand in key markets, particularly in North America. Investment responds to a stable policy environment.

Reported Figures and Their Context

The 4.4% first-half figure is an accumulated measure, not an annualized rate. It shows total growth from January through June 2026.

The IMAE’s June reading of 4.2% year over year indicates a slight acceleration. That is up from 3.9% in the same month last year.

These figures come from Banguat’s official statistics, reported widely on 21 and 22 August. No other growth figures were published in the reports.

Comparisons with past years show a steady recovery pattern. The data underscores the resilience of the Central American economy.

Guatemala’s growth rate positions it as a standout performer in Central America. Many regional peers struggle with slower expansion or fiscal challenges.

The 4.4% pace suggests healthy domestic demand and external linkages. This could attract investor attention to the country’s market.

Regional analysts often highlight Guatemala’s macroeconomic stability as a plus. The current data reinforces that reputation with concrete numbers.

Sustained growth also supports government revenue collection. That revenue can fund public services and infrastructure projects.

Outlook and Monitoring Ahead

Banguat’s revised GDP forecast signals optimism for the rest of 2026. The central bank sees current trends continuing through the year.

Monitoring the IMAE monthly will show if momentum holds. A slowdown in any key sector could affect the full-year outcome.

Remittance flows and global demand for exports remain watch items. These external factors can shift quickly and impact economic performance.

For now, the first-half data points to a solid year ahead. Guatemala growth appears set to remain a positive regional story.

Uruguay · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Montevideo’s Casino Parque Hotel closes as a municipal casino on 28 August 2026 and transfers to national control.

— How big The casino has 46 workers, with 35 taking early retirement and 11 moving to other municipal jobs.

— The catch The building, inaugurated in 1909, has operated from Casa de Andalucía only since 2015, not its original site.

— Who pays The Intendencia de Montevideo ends its subsidised operation after the casino posted losses in 2024.

— What comes next The Ministry of Economy reopens the casino around 9-10 September 2026 with its own staff.

— Investment note IBF Negocios has invested over US$200 million in Uruguayan companies over 15 years.

Uruguay’s only municipal casino moves under national control from September, as investment firm IBF Negocios expands.

Montevideo’s Casino Parque Hotel, Uruguay’s only municipal casino, will close on Friday 28 August 2026 after years of losses. The national Ministry of Economy and Finance takes possession on 1 September 2026 and will reopen it days later.

Casino chips (illustrative); the Casino Parque Hotel concession passes to Uruguay’s finance ministry on 1 September.

Why the Casino Parque Hotel leaves municipal hands

The Casino Parque Hotel is Uruguay’s only municipal casino, housed in the Casa de Andalucía building in Parque Rodó. The Intendencia de Montevideo, the city government, has managed it for years, but the operation has run persistent deficits.

In 2024, the casino posted losses, described in Spanish as ‘números en rojo,’ meaning red numbers. That financial performance convinced city officials the casino was no longer sustainable as a municipal business.

A formal resolution ends municipal management, transferring the building and casino operation to the national Ministry of Economy and Finance. The ministry will take possession from 1 September 2026, according to reports from 21 August 2026.

El País reported on 21 August 2026 that the decision follows successive deficit balances. The transfer reclassifies Casino Parque Hotel from a municipal casino to a national one under existing state regulations.

The legal and administrative background of the transfer

The Intendencia de Montevideo issued a resolution to end its management and transfer the property to the Ministry of Economy and Finance. This starts a formal process called ‘toma de posesión,’ meaning taking possession, from September onward.

Historically, the Parque Hotel building opened in 1909, and the city government acquired it in 1915. In 2015, casino operations moved from the historic building into the Casa de Andalucía premises, where they currently function.

State casinos in Uruguay operate under the Dirección General de Casinos, an agency under the Ministry of Economy and Finance. This agency already manages casinos at Nogaró, Victoria Plaza, Piriápolis, Rivera, and 31 gaming halls nationwide.

Group R Multimedio reported on 21 August 2026 the historical details and the resolution’s content. The transfer brings Casino Parque Hotel under the same regulatory framework governing other national casinos.

What happens from 1 September 2026

Casino Parque Hotel closes as a municipal casino on Friday 28 August 2026. The Ministry of Economy and Finance takes possession of the building on 1 September 2026.

The casino is expected to reopen under national management around 9 or 10 September 2026. New staff, hired by the national casino authority, will operate the gaming floor.

Montevideo Portal reported on 21 August 2026 the planned reopening date and new staffing. The venue remains an emblematic casino point in Parque Rodó, now part of the national network.

Subrayado confirmed on 21 August 2026 the possession date and operational shift. The building itself is not being repurposed away from gaming, just changing management.

Workers face retirement or reallocation

Casino Parque Hotel currently employs 46 workers under the Montevideo municipality. A negotiated agreement between the city and the workers’ union settles their future.

Thirty-five workers will take early retirement, called ‘retiro anticipado,’ with economic incentives. Their years of service count as ‘insalubres,’ meaning unhealthy work, allowing retirement at a lower age.

The remaining 11 workers will move to other municipal jobs, the Adeom municipal workers’ union said.

Pablo Nisivoccia, vice-president of the Association of State Casino Workers, noted new staff will arrive with the Ministry. The casino reopens under state management in early September, as reported by Subrayado on 21 August 2026.

The hotel building and its future use

The Casino Parque Hotel building, an emblematic structure in Parque Rodó, ceases to be a municipal asset from 1 September 2026. The national Dirección General de Casinos assumes operational control of the gaming operation.

This agency will use its own personnel to run the casino, according to Grupo R Multimedio on 21 August 2026. The venue stays as a casino, integrated into the state-run network across Uruguay.

Available reports focus on the casino use and labor aspects, not on any separate hotel-lodging business. The current activity is described as a municipal casino in Casa de Andalucía, without mention of overnight guests.

The main change is institutional and operational, from municipal to national control. El País reported on 21 August 2026 that the building remains in gaming use, not repurposed away from it.

IBF Negocios and its US$200 million investment

IBF Negocios, an investment firm, marks 15 years of activity in Uruguay in 2026. Over this period, it has invested more than US$200 million in Uruguayan companies, according to Ámbito on 24 August 2026.

The firm began around 2011 with seven or eight founding partners. It has since grown to about 600 investors participating in its investment vehicles.

Since roughly 2021-2022, IBF accelerated its pace, investing between US$40 million and US$50 million per year. This marks a clear shift from its earlier, more gradual growth phase.

As of 2026, companies in IBF’s portfolio collectively generate over US$250 million in annual sales. The firm has built a diversified set of holdings across the Uruguayan economy.

Sectors targeted by IBF Negocios

IBF Negocios operates across several real-sector and consumer-oriented industries. These include food, agribusiness, veterinary products, technology, and mass-consumption goods.

The firm’s strategy involves diversifying its acquisitions across different economic segments. This approach spreads risk and captures growth in various Uruguayan markets.

Ámbito reported on 24 August 2026 the full list of sectors in IBF’s portfolio. The firms in these industries range from small enterprises to larger companies.

The acceleration since 2021-2022 allowed IBF to add broader and larger companies. This fits a pattern of aggressive expansion in the country’s investment landscape.

A concrete deal: IBF joins Edintor S.A.

IBF Negocios has taken an equity stake in Edintor S.A., an importer and distributor in Uruguay. This company distributes INGCO, a leading brand in the local tools market.

The association aims to ‘acelerar su expansión en Uruguay y la región,’ meaning accelerate its expansion. IBF adds Edintor as a new company to its portfolio, according to a business note from 20 August 2026.

Public summaries focus on strategy and aggregate numbers, not listing all portfolio companies. Edintor S.A. stands as one confirmed example of IBF’s concrete investments.

The deal supports Edintor’s growth plans within Uruguay and the wider region. This fits IBF’s pattern of backing firms in distribution and consumer-facing sectors.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Casino Parque Hotel close as a municipal casino? Casino Parque Hotel closes on Friday 28 August 2026. The Ministry of Economy and Finance takes possession from 1 September 2026. Why is the casino being transferred to the national government? The casino has run persistent deficits, including losses in 2024. The Intendencia de Montevideo decided it was no longer financially sustainable as a municipal operation. What happens to the casino’s 46 workers? Thirty-five workers take early retirement with incentives, counting their service as unhealthy work. The remaining 11 workers move to other municipal jobs. Will the casino reopen under new management? Yes, the casino reopens around 9 or 10 September 2026. The national Dirección General de Casinos will run it with new staff. What does IBF Negocios have to do with the casino? IBF Negocios is a separate investment firm, not related to the casino. It has invested over US$200 million in Uruguayan companies over 15 years.
