There is no documented evidence of a political link between Gilauri’s public criticism, the acceleration of the court proceedings and the final ruling. However, the chronology raises questions. The trial court concluded a four-year dispute about two months after Gilauri made a series of high-profile political statements. The higher courts then reviewed the extensive case file within eight months.

The state has now sold Gilauri’s house at auction. The former prime minister remains silent, while authorities continue to pursue his assets and business interests to recover the money.

Nika Gilauri case

World.title: Aliyev’s Uzbekistan visit: ‘Eternal friendship’ and family business expansion
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Uzbekistan

The state visit to Tashkent was presented by official media as a “new, symbolic and practical stage” in relations between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.

Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev held a one-on-one meeting, chaired the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council, signed a “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”, awarded each other their countries’ highest state honours, and took part in ceremonies marking the opening and laying of foundations for Azerbaijani investment projects in Uzbekistan.

However, behind the official statements and rhetoric about “brotherhood” lie specific financial and business interests. Against the backdrop of the visit, attention has also focused on the parallel expansion of private companies directly or indirectly linked to Ilham Aliyev’s family, including PASHA Holding and Emin Agalarov’s Sea Breeze project.

What happened?

The main document signed during the visit was the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship”. Under the treaty, the two sides intend to build relations based on the principles of eternal friendship, mutual trust, strategic partnership and alliance, as well as support each other’s national development models. They undertake not to join blocs or alliances that could harm the other side’s sovereignty, security or territorial integrity, and not to allow their territory to be used by third parties for such purposes or for the activities of such groups.

Areas of cooperation outlined in the treaty include strengthening the UN’s central role, developing interparliamentary ties, trade and investment, including in energy, transport and logistics, digital development, agriculture, the green and digital economies, e-commerce, ICT and space technologies. The treaty also provides for the development of interconnected transport systems, the preservation of cultural and humanitarian ties, language learning, scientific and educational exchanges, interregional cooperation and tourism.

The heads of state exchanged their countries’ highest state honours, with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev receiving the Heydar Aliyev Order. Ceremonies were also held to open and lay the foundations for specific Azerbaijani projects in Uzbekistan, including hotel and residential complexes, tourism facilities, a building for the Nizami Ganjavi University, an “Azerbaijan” park and other facilities.

Joint projects have been launched in banking and finance, construction materials production, education, the oil and gas sector, tourism, housing construction, mining and agriculture. A corresponding “road map” was also adopted.

Azerbaijan’s state-owned bank enters Uzbek market

President Ilham Aliyev cited several specific examples of cooperation, including the entry of a leading Azerbaijani bank into the Uzbek market, the expansion of SOCAR’s retail network, oil and gas exploration nearing its final stage, and the prospect of drilling production wells next year.

The bank in question is the International Bank of Azerbaijan (ABB), the country’s largest state-owned bank, with around 88–92% of its shares held by the Finance Ministry and other state bodies. ABB is acquiring a 51% controlling stake in the privately owned Uzbek bank Davr Bank, investing more than $100m in the deal.

Despite its state-owned status, ABB was previously implicated in the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal, involving a $2.9bn money-laundering scheme. The bank is now entering the Uzbek market with the backing of state resources and political will. The deal is being presented as a purely commercial decision, but comes against the backdrop of a strengthening political alliance between the two countries.

Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov announced the deal at an interregional forum a day before the visit, and it was formally concluded on the day of the visit. ABB will operate in Uzbekistan under the Davr Bank brand. The bank has assets of around $1bn, a customer base of 1.4 million and a network of 43 branches. Fitch Ratings expects the deal to be completed by the fourth quarter of 2026.

Expansion of businesses linked to Aliyev family

Alongside the official banking deal, several private projects have also attracted attention during the visit and in the preceding period. Some are linked to companies and structures directly or indirectly associated with the president’s family.

Sea Breeze Uzbekistan: A $5bn resort project being developed by Agalarov Development, owned by Emin Agalarov, the former husband of President Aliyev’s daughter Leyla Aliyeva. The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support.

The complex is planned for a 577-hectare site on the shores of the Charvak Reservoir. In 2025, the project was presented directly to Mirziyoyev and fast-tracked without a tender, while the environmental assessment had not yet been fully completed. A foundation-laying ceremony took place on the day of the visit. Although Agalarov is no longer related to the presidential family by marriage, he continues to enjoy high-level political support. PASHA Holding projects: The holding company, which has been linked to the president’s daughters Leyla and Arzu Aliyeva, as well as to Mehriban Aliyeva’s father Arif Pashayev, is building a Ritz-Carlton-branded hotel and residential complex in Tashkent. The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates.

The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Heydar Aliyev Center illuminated in colors of Ukrainian flag
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku has been illuminated in the colors of the Ukrainian national flag.

Ukrainian Ambassador to Azerbaijan Yuriy Husyev shared the information on his social media account.

“Baku tonight is special! Thank you, Azerbaijan!” the post said.

August 24 marks Ukraine’s Independence Day, the country’s main national holiday. It commemorates the adoption by the Verkhovna Rada of the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine on August 24, 1991. The decision was subsequently confirmed by a nationwide referendum on December 1 of the same year.

World.title: Video produced on President Ilham Aliyev’s state visit to Uzbekistan (VIDEO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. A video has been produced on President Ilham Aliyev’s state visit to Uzbekistan, featuring footage of the head of state’s participation in events in the cities of Tashkent and Bukhara.

Trend reports that the video, prepared by the Presidential Press Service, also includes footage of President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva visiting the Independence Monument in Tashkent and laying bouquets of flowers before the bas-relief of National Leader Heydar Aliyev at Heydar Aliyev Square.

The footage also shows the official welcoming ceremony for the President of Azerbaijan at the Kuksaroy State Residence in Tashkent, the head of state’s one-on-one meeting with his Uzbek counterpart, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, as well as his participation online in the opening and groundbreaking ceremonies of joint projects.

The video also features the ceremony for the signing and exchange of documents between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. In addition, it includes footage of Ilham Aliyev being briefed on Uzbekistan’s largest urban development project, “New Tashkent.”

The video also shows the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, the ceremony at which the presidents were presented with awards, statements by Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev to the press, and the opening of the Nizami Ganjavi National Pedagogical University.

The video continues with President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva’s trip from Tashkent to Bukhara. In Bukhara, it also features their visits to the Ismail Samani Mausoleum, the Ark Fortress, and the Poi-Kalyan complex.

The footage concludes with the end of the President’s state visit to Uzbekistan.

World.title: NRL changes rules to allow Jai Arrow to 'play' 100 games for Souths
World.content:
Jai Arrow will make cameo appearances in the final two rounds of the regular season in order to reach 100 games for South Sydney.

In one of the feel-good stories of the NRL season, the forward who retired with motor neurone disease in May has been approved to start on the field in rounds 26 and 27.

Arrow will then be substituted out in the opening seconds before any active involvement in play.

It came after the Rabbitohs made an appeal to the NRL to grant the former Queensland representative an on-field swansong while still able to walk and run.

The initiative gives Arrow two final chances to farewell an NRL career that featured a grand-final appearance in 2021 and 12 State of Origin caps.

The NRL has granted Souths special dispensation to name Arrow as an extra player on today's team list and an extra substitution in their rotation.

Arrow vows to help others fight MND Former NRL player Jai Arrow says he is determined to raise money and awareness for Motor Neurone Disease until a cure is found.

The matches, against Gold Coast and the Sydney Roosters, will bring Arrow's tally to 180 career games and 100 for the Rabbitohs.

Arrow will lead the team out on both occasions and sit on the interchange bench in Souths kit after being substituted out.

The Titans and Roosters have both approved the plan, as have the Rugby League Players Association.

"We are very grateful to Peter [V'landys] and the NRL, and Clint [Newton] at the RLPA, for supporting our proposal," Souths chief executive Blake Solly said.

"We believe this will provide great inspiration for everyone watching the game from the stadium or at home, showing that MND will not hold Jai, or anyone else, back from achieving what they want to achieve in life."

The NRL world has rallied around Arrow since his shock diagnosis and immediate retirement in May.

The league threw Arrow "the world's biggest birthday party" on the day Souths beat Newcastle in July, rolling out a birthday cake in the shape of the 31-year-old's jersey and presenting him with a commemorative jersey.

Fundraising efforts have already passed $1 million in support of Arrow, who is the father of a young daughter.

Players from all clubs have shown their support by marking tries with arrow celebrations throughout the month of July.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Breaking: Second case of H5 bird flu confirmed in Queensland
World.content:
Queensland has recorded its second case of H5 avian flu after a dead migratory seabird tested positive on the Sunshine Coast.

The wild shearwater found dead at Castaways Beach returned a positive result for the disease from the Queensland Government's biosecurity science laboratory last night.

The first case was on Moreton Island in late July.

Primary Industries Minister Tony Perrett has told parliament protecting the state's multi-million dollar poultry sector is the government's top priority.

World.title: Man accused of murdering 78yo during crime spree remains in custody
World.content:
A man accused of beating a 78-year-old man to death with a metal pole and injuring two other men remains in custody in Queensland.

Richard Zoltan Babos, 36, was not present when his matters were mentioned in the Bundaberg Magistrates Court today.

He is charged with multiple offences, including murder, attempted murder, and acts intended to maim or disfigure.

The charges relate to a crime spree Mr Babos is alleged to have carried out around the Queensland town of Childers, 300 kilometres north of Brisbane, in May this year.

Police allege Richard Babos assaulted two men in separate incidents at North and Crescent streets. (ABC News)

Police allege Mr Babos had been driving along North Street at about 2:30pm on May 27 when he reversed into several cars.

One of the drivers, a 65-year-old Howard man, got out of his car to inspect the damage and Mr Babos allegedly reversed into him and punched him several times before leaving the scene.

Police say Mr Babos then travelled to Whitebridge Road in North Isis, where he allegedly punched 78-year-old Lawrence Elliott in the head before hitting him with a metal pole.

Mr Elliott died at the scene.

Police said Mr Babos then drove to Crescent Street in Childers, where he allegedly assaulted a 66-year-old man.

Mr Babos was taken into custody after being restrained by bystanders.

Police say Lawrence Elliott was killed while walking along Whitebridge Road. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

DNA delays

Mr Babos's lawyer, Jackie Lynch, told the court she had received a brief of evidence on August 18, but that there were some outstanding matters, including scientific evidence.

Police prosecutor Leon Casey told the court DNA results were "taking a long time".

He said it would be a 12- month wait for the DNA evidence, but Magistrate Stephen Byrne asked for the matter to be adjourned to later this year.

The case will return to court on December 15.

World.title: Energy efficiency business accused of fraud by Victorian authorities
World.content:
A Victorian business business has been accused of submitting doctored photos and falsifying customer details to claim certificates for energy efficiency projects.

Royal One Pty Ltd has had its Victorian Energy Upgrades (VEU) program accreditation suspended by the state's Essential Services Commission.

The business promoted itself as a provider of energy efficient air conditioning, hot water and solar and battery power on its website.

The commission's fraud taskforce said some photos submitted by Royal One as evidence of energy efficiency upgrades had been digitally altered.

The commission also said phone audits of Royal One's listed consumers provided further evidence of attempted fraud.

The VEU program is an energy efficiency scheme designed to help people lower their energy bills by increasing efficiency.

Labor and the Coalition offer two very different plans for Victoria's energy supply The Labor government has signed a deal for $7.6 billion powerline, while the Coalition has hardened its stance to block the project.

Accredited businesses that carry out the energy efficiency improvements can earn certificates which they can then sell to energy retailers.

Royal One's VEU accreditation expired shortly after it was suspended and the business has not applied to renew it.

Essential Services Commission chairperson and commissioner Gerard Brody said the commission was alerted to Royal One's alleged fraud.

"The taskforce uses data, tip-offs and other intelligence to identify areas of unusual activity and in this case, uncovered what we allege to be deliberate and fraudulent conduct from Royal One," he said.

"Immediately suspending Royal One directly affected their ability to generate income from the VEU program.

" The message is clear — deliberately breaking the rules puts your business at risk. "

Royal One has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Charter guide spots foreign fishing boat, crew detained
World.content:
Australian Border Force (ABF) has seized a suspected foreign fishing boat off Queensland's northern tip and detained its crew.

Albany Island Fishing Tours owner Dave Hartwell said he reported the boat to ABF after one of the company's guides spotted it on Little Adolphus Island, in the southern Torres Strait, late last week.

Mr Hartwell said the guide saw "about seven" people on board walking around the boat.

"He sort of offered… [asked] if they needed any immediate assistance, asked if they needed water," Mr Hartwell said.

"He was a bit shocked, actually, rang me so we could report it straight away.

"The phone service is pretty dodgy out there."

In a statement on Tuesday, Border Force said it found the boat and crew near Little Adolphus Island on Friday after reports from the community.

A fishing boat was seized near Little Adolphus Island in the Torres Strait on Friday. (Supplied: Australian Border Force)

Its officers boarded the boat and identified evidence of suspected illegal fishing, including fishing equipment and 700 kilograms of salt used to preserve catch.

Border Force said the boat was "located before any marine life was caught".

It said the crew would be taken to Darwin for further investigation by the Australian Fisheries Management Authority, for suspected offences against the Torres Strait Fisheries Act 1984.

Border Force said it was working with partner agencies "to determine the appropriate management" of the boat.

So far this year, 14 of the 24 suspected illegal foreign fishing boats caught in Far North Queensland waters have been destroyed, Border Force said.

Boats make locals anxious

Mr Hartwell said the boat was spotted about seven nautical miles north-east of Pajinka, the tip of Cape York Peninsula.

"It was an incredibly fast response [from Border Force] … it would be nice if no boats came in."

"It wasn't a very big boat, maybe 30 foot long or 35."

Mr Hartwell said he had seen an increased Border Force presence in the Torres Strait since a dedicated operation was launched in February in response to an influx of illegal fishing boats in the Torres Strait.

An Australian Border Force vessel arrived to the island where the foreign boat had been spotted. (Supplied: Dave Hartwell)

"I don't know what they can do to help but maybe a bit more in the air, or maybe some intel from [Indonesia]… find out where they are coming from," he said.

Mr Hartwell said those living in the isolated communities around the remote islands were anxious about the boats because "you just don't know what they're all about".

In late June, a boat carrying foreign nationals made landfall north of Weipa, on western Cape York Peninsula, which led to two men being charged with people smuggling.

"We're a long way from any police, emergency response or anything if we're in trouble," Mr Hartwell said.

" It would probably take at [the] very minimum, a helicopter or boat an hour to get here if we were in strife. "

Maritime Border Command deputy commander Natasha O'Farrell thanked the community members who reported the boat.

An Albany Island fishing charter company spotted the boat sinking in the water. (Supplied: Dave Hartwell)

"Communities across the Torres Strait are vital eyes and ears and one part of a layered approach that includes aerial surveillance, patrol vessels, land patrols and intelligence operations," she said.

"Illegal fishing activity can fluctuate, but our resolve does not.

"If you enter Australian waters to fish illegally, you risk losing your catch, your equipment and your vessel, and you may face prosecution."

World.title: Sledgehammers and explosives more common in museum heists, Europol says
World.content:
Sledgehammers, axes, and explosives are the new weapons of choice for thieves targeting European museums, according to a report by police agency Europol.

Museum heists were becoming increasingly aggressive, the report said, taking on "violent and forceful" methods.

It's a stark contrast to prior "discreet" thefts, where perpetrators relied on deception, stealth and reconnaissance.

In 2024, a large-scale theft of valuable books from libraries across the European Union (EU) saw perpetrators replace the originals with counterfeit copies to avoid detection.

Two years on, Europol said there had been a shift towards more "direct and confrontational" tactics.

"In some cases, offenders use firearms to intimidate security personnel and visitors," the agency's report said.

"Some museum thefts have involved direct physical assaults on staff, such as tying them up or using brute force against them.

"[The] use of force is closely linked to targeted operations, suggesting prior identification of specific objects and pre-planned execution."

The 2025 Louvre heist remains unsolved

Europol's report cited several examples of violent thefts, including the attack on the Louvre Museum in Paris in 2025.

Surveillance footage of the heist showed thieves smashing glass display cases and taking the jewellery inside.

The heist, which made international headlines, took less than eight minutes.

New footage of Louvre heist released The security footage shows the thieves smashing the glass on the display cases where the jewellery was kept.

The four thieves spent only four minutes inside the museum itself, entering via a crane to the gallery window.

The estimated value of the stolen jewellery was about $US102 million ($156 million).

Only one man has been charged to date, and none of the jewels have been located.

The targeting of precious metals and stones was another cultural shift noted by Europol.

"Most of these incidents involved some degree of violence," the report said.

" Thieves have stolen golden objects, such as nuggets, gold coins, golden decorative pieces as well as jewels with precious stones. "

Loading...

The report also noted Chinese cultural artefacts were repeatedly being targeted, including Ming Dynasty vases and porcelain plates from the 12th-13th centuries.

Changing market demand for museum thefts

Precious metals stolen from museums can be melted down, according to the report, leaving no trace.

Precious stones can be removed and sold on.

"Both types of items are attractive to criminal networks due to their visibility, accessibility, and the perception that museum security measures are less robust than those in jewellery stores," the report said.

"Similarly, ancient Chinese porcelain artefacts are likely targeted by cultural goods traffickers for financial gain.

"Driven by high demand, they are likely to be easily sold on the art market."

In 2019, thieves targeted Germany's Green Vault city palace. (Reuters: Matthias Rietschel)

The shift towards violent means in the pursuit of specific items or cultural goods could indicate a newer kind of thief.

Typically, Europol's report said, goods traffickers would avoid violence.

These newer thieves often have a history of involvement in other types of crime, and some appear to coordinate their heists on an "ad hoc basis".

"[They are] often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other," Europol's report said.

"It is possible that low-level executors of thefts are randomly recruited on a crime-as-a-service basis.

"Alternatively, some criminal actors and networks … [have] realised the low-risk, high-profit potential of museum heists."

World.title: Good character references to be scrapped in all WA criminal cases
World.content:
The ability for convicted criminals to rely on good character references from family, friends and colleagues to reduce their sentences will be banned in Western Australia, after three government employees were stood down for supporting a former colleague convicted of rape.

The WA government has rushed to ban the practice after revelations three Western Power staff provided references to a senior manager who was jailed for raping a former colleague on a work trip.

Currently, judges can reduce the sentences of convicted criminals based on character references provided to the court.

Work had already been underway to end the practice in child abuse cases, but the Cook government was pushed into taking further action after the Western Power saga was made public.

Jeffrey David Spinner, 59, was sentenced to five years in jail after taking a female colleague to his hotel room when she was heavily intoxicated in 2024, and assaulting her.

Court transcripts included eight positive character references from his colleagues which the judge found indicated the rape was "out of character".

Western Power employee Jeffrey David Spinner (right) was in June sentenced to five years in jail for the rape of a colleague in 2024. (Facebook: Jeff Spinner)

One Western Power colleague said Spinner had always acted "respectfully and appropriately" towards her and others, while another described him as having a "strong moral compass".

Three of those colleagues have been stood down, pending a review ordered by Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson, after media reporting brought the case to light.

'Favourable' treatment

Attorney-General Tony Buti said legislation currently being drafted would now be expanded to ban references for all crimes.

"This is important reform [and] was already well advanced for child abuse cases," he said in a statement.

"Expanding it to ban character references for other sentencing hearings is an important next step."

Tony Buti says the changes will apply to all criminal cases. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A government statement noted there had been "growing concern" about a perception people with "professional standing, community status or strong personal networks" were getting "favourable" treatment as a result of good character references.

The state's leading family and sexual violence advocate had warned the practice allowed unreliable evidence into courtrooms and risked making victims feel they were to blame.

Case highlights 'significant concern'

A snap review of the Western Power case, and the utility's handling of the matter, was expected to be completed around the start of this week.

Western Power staff stood down after backing manager in rape trial Western Australia's energy minister lashes out at Western Power employees who provided references for a senior manager who was jailed for raping a female colleague.

Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said the case had highlighted "significant concern" about the use of good character references.

"It is clear that the public doesn't support good character references. I don't support them either," she said in a statement.

"Put simply — convicted criminals shouldn't have the benefit of glowing references when it comes to sentencing.

"Today's announcement is a sensible move which will ensure our court processes meet community expectations and bring WA into line with other jurisdictions."

New South Wales has banned character references in sexual offences cases only.

In February the Victorian government announced it planned to scrap good character references in all cases.

World.title: Queensland bail breach laws to carry minimum 12 month jail sentence
World.content:
Serious repeat offenders, charged under the Queensland state government's proposed breach bail, go to jail laws will face a mandatory minimum sentence of 12 months behind bars.

Premier David Crisafulli confirmed the legislation, which is set to be introduced in parliament this week, will apply to both youths and adults.

The proposed laws would create a new offence, which a judge or magistrate can choose to apply to offenders who commit a crime captured under adult crime, adult time (ACAT) laws.

There are 47 offences under the ACAT legislation, including murder, manslaughter, robbery and rape.

The government's adult crime, adult time legislation was a key election campaign policy for the LNP. (ABC News: Cameron Simmons)

David Crisafulli said the crackdown would mean Queensland would have the strongest bail laws in the nation.

"These laws aren't about the unlucky first-time offender," the premier said.

"They are about the repeat offender who has already been before a court, who has been granted bail and who knows their conditions and who makes the choice to go out and commit another serious offence."

Youth Justice Minister Laura Gerber said the proposed laws were about the "rights of victims".

"Bail is a privilege, it is not a right," Ms Gerber said.

Laura Gerber speaking about "breach bail, go to jail" laws in Townsville. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"If these repeat offenders are breaching it, they should go to jail under the next phase of adult crime, adult time."

Police Minister Dan Purdie said frontline officers had been calling for bail reform for some time and were frustrated by "a revolving door" of youth offenders.

"[They are] arrested in the morning and released to offend again in the afternoon," Mr Purdie said.

"They call it catch and release. That ends with breach bail, go to jail."

The Queensland government's proposal expands its signature adult time, adult crime policy. (ABC News: Ned Hammond)

Youth Advocacy Centre CEO Katherine Hayes said the government's approach was going to create worse outcomes for victims of crime.

"We're doubling down on the system that doesn't work, which is really big detention centres that end up being crime factories," she said.

"They jam kids in, they can't be properly staffed, they don't have access to proper rehabilitation, they're not having access to education and they come out and continue to offend is the bottom line."

Katherine Hayes says this approach is going to create worse outcomes for victims of crime. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Overcrowding is a major concern for youth detention centre workers, who this morning returned to their jobs from a 24-hour strike.

Negotiations with the government over pay, staffing shortages and safety concerns, have broken down.

The Australian Workers Union yesterday said all youth detention centres across the state were at capacity, and a further 40 children were sitting in watch houses, waiting for a bed.

Before the bail reform changes, Queensland Corrective Services (QCS) was already forecasting the number of extra prisoners in the system to increase by between 1,500 and 5,200 by June 2035.

Almost two in three youth offenders offending on bail, government says Mandatory minimum sentences for youth offenders who breach bail.

"I'd rather have less crooks in a cell, than in your lounge room," the premier told parliament today.

Ms Hayes said the proposed laws treated the symptom, not the cause.

"The problem will continue because it's the same model of detention — the large centre, the inability to staff the centre properly — and then we still won't be able to rehabilitate," she said.

"We stop [youth crime] occurring by addressing the root causes, which is looking at poverty, homes where there is violence, there's drug use, almost all of the children that are serious repeat offenders have experienced some level of abuse and come from homes that have violence, and are disengaged from education."

World.title: The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview Jon Pierik August 25, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When James Hird said his goodbyes after finishing his challenging interview before the panel charged with finding Essendon’s new coach, he was buoyant. On two fronts. According to a senior industry figure with knowledge of the Bombers’ interviewing process, the former premiership captain and club great felt as if he had done all he could to reclaim a role he cherished, and one he had held proudly more than a decade ago before trouble struck. Mark McVeigh (left) and James Hird with the Bombers in 2004. Getty Images But, just as importantly, he was also satisfied the Bombers had run a thorough process, where he was given the freedom to push his case, but – on the flipside – was spared no leniency. That’s why, amid the disappointment of being overlooked in favour of great mate Mark McVeigh, Hird cannot complain.



“From a personal point of view though, it’s very disappointing,” Hird said on Nine’s Footy Furnace after it was confirmed that he, like Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide coaching director Murray Davis, had missed out on the job. “Yeah, I’m disappointed, put my heart and soul into the effort, but, obviously, fell short and that’s the way it goes.” Loading Before facing the selection committee of chief executive Tim Roberts, president Andrew Welsh, vice-president Anthony Di Pietro, board member and former Swans player Ted Richards and people and culture executive Caroline Monzon, Hird had felt the one issue that may torpedo his bid to return was the hangover from the supplements’ saga all those years ago, the same source said. However, Hird felt he had moved on as best he could. McVeigh was one of the 34 players suspended for the 2016 season. Over the years since, Hird has met with many of the 34 who had sought answers, and Hird provided them with as much clarity as he could.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach There were a couple who still harboured frustration, but Hird, according to the same senior source, had left those deep conversations believing the two parties were now on better terms. This process was relayed to Welsh when he asked Hird about his relationships with those former players, according to the same senior industry source. Welsh declined to discuss specifics of the interview when asked about this on Tuesday. Hird was pushed and challenged through the Bombers’ detailed process, as were all the candidates.



Late in his pivotal interview, Hird, according to two sources with knowledge of the meeting, asked the panel: “What concerns have you got about me being the coach?” Roberts said he had wondered whether Hird was “bigger than the club”. But Roberts and the rest of the panel agreed in the end that their concerns on that front had been extinguished. Ted Richards, the club’s football director, and a former teammate who went on to be a Sydney Swans’ premiership player, told Hird that successful coaches typically come from a top-four or top-six team and have experience at multiple clubs. Hird did not. Hird and McVeigh at Essendon in 2010. Getty Images Hird politely reminded the questioner that he had been captain of the best team of his era, the dominant 2000 premiership side, and, in his first stint as coach, the Bombers had played off for top spot on the ladder in round 14, 2013.



As this masthead has reported, Hird has also made it clear he had been involved in high-performance environments in the years since, including the business world, and you don’t need to follow the “typical linear” model to succeed. Hird had briefly been an assistant coach at Greater Western Sydney when McVeigh was caretaker coach, and is now director of coaching at VFL club, Port Melbourne. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move He had seen how the game – and coaching – had changed, the attention span of youngers players becoming shorter and shorter in this modern, social-media driven age. Rather than long sermons, Hird had seen the importance of sound-bites, and the use of artificial intelligence. Hird was asked how he would handle major media issues. The panel acknowledged that what Hird said, because of his huge standing in the game, let alone the club, carried tremendous weight, so if he broke ranks, the club could be destabilised.



Hird responded that he would always consult the president and chief executive, and would fall into line behind what the club wanted, regardless of his own view. Soccer great Kevin Muscat was used by the Bombers to scrutinise the applicants’ gameplan and strategy, although this was an open-ended question because applicants needed more details on the opponent they may have been playing and conditions at the venue. For anyone who has listened to Hird weekly on his football shows on Nine, the owner of this masthead, Hird has been big on having a team outnumber an opponent at the contest, and then run, spread and attack – as is the modern way. However, Welsh said McVeigh had the better plan. Andrew Welsh (second from left) and McVeigh (second from right) in their playing days. Paul Rovere “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage,” Welsh said.



“His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading.” Hird believed he was the best applicant for the job. As did all the applicants, otherwise why would they have applied? The Bombers may yet seek to bring him back inside the tent in a prominent role, but Hird craved the senior coaching role, and may be unwilling. Welsh said on Tuesday he was keen to catch up with Hird and would love to see him at Essendon in some capacity. A twist in the tale would be if Hird joined another club, raising eyebrows on Sunday when he said rivals had reached out to him. Hird has repeatedly said he wants what’s best for the Bombers, a one-time power that has fallen on hard and miserable times and just completed its worst season. As former club president Lindsay Tanner said, the job of all Essendon people now is to unite behind the new coach. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Fortescue stands down executive at the centre of harassment probe
World.content:
Mining giant Fortescue has moved to suspend a senior executive from working for the company while allegations of sexual harassment and bullying are being investigated by law firm MinterEllison.

Just last week, the West Australia miner defended its decision not to stand down the executive at the centre of the investigation while the probe was underway, saying it had taken extensive external legal and governance advice to come to that decision.

The mining giant is investigating a serious allegation against a senior executive at the company. Bloomberg

But on Tuesday Fortescue said the employee will be suspended. “It has been decided that the employee who is the subject of the allegations will not undertake any work for Fortescue while the investigation continues,” a spokesperson said.

“The investigation is ongoing and no findings have been made. Sexual harassment, unlawful discrimination and any behaviour that makes people feel unsafe have no place at Fortescue,” they said.

World.title: Major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses, placing buyers in limbo
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWInsolvency Major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses, placing buyers in limbo Ellie Busby and Anthony Segaert Updated August 25, 2026 — 11:39am ,first published 10:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Embattled western Sydney housing developer Bathla Group has collapsed into voluntary administration, leaving hundreds of buyers who purchased off-the-plan homes in limbo. Documents filed with the corporate regulator on Tuesday morning reveal Teneo has been appointed as administrator of the company, and its hundreds of related entities including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction. Bathla Group has collapsed. Louie Douvis In an Instagram post on the company’s page, founder and director Bhart Bhushan described the voluntary administration as the “orderly restructure of business” and blamed the decision on “a perfect storm” of declining sales, rising construction costs and the federal government’s May budget. “Our first thoughts are with our employees and the customers who have put their faith in us to deliver their dream of home ownership,” he said. “It is my sincere hope this process can allow that to happen by working collaboratively with the administrators, our suppliers, contractors and lending partners.”



In a statement, Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said the company recognised it was a “difficult situation” and said the appointment of administrators was “in the best interest of all stakeholders”. “The business has been through a period of declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased,” he said. “We will work constructively with the administrators to support the continued delivery of much-needed housing for western Sydney.” The collapse has left buyers who purchased off the plan unsure about what to do. Last week the Herald reported that buyers who had purchased apartments off the plan at Bathla’s Kembla Grange development had been unable to move in after the completion date for the project, which was originally slated for December 2025, had been extended four times. Janice Cahill, who bought an apartment at the development, said the delays have “really and truly” affected her mental health. When Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September last year, she found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces.



On Tuesday morning she called her real estate agent, asking what the collapse meant, and was assured the project was continuing. Building Commission NSW, the state’s construction watchdog, has undertaken more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites over the past few months. It identified defects at the Kembla Grange development. When asked why the completion date for the project had been pushed back, the spokesperson for Bathla said it was “due to unforeseen site delays with some external works … Completion is forecast for November”. Janice Cahill is hoping to move in to her new home later this year. Wolter Peeters On Friday, Building Commission NSW confirmed it had issued penalties and imposed extensive licence conditions on Raj & Jai Construction and its director, after finding they engaged in improper conduct.



It found the company had carried out work at two properties in Schofields without the mandatory Home Building Compensation Fund (HBCF) insurance being in place, and that its director, on behalf of Raj & Jai Construction, made misleading statements in the applications for the two HBCF insurance certificates. Raj & Jai Construction was fined $45,000, and its director, $9000. “I accept that that’s not [a huge penalty] but these penalties were for these two particular offences and they were proportionate to those offences,” Building Commissioner James Sherrard told budget estimates on Monday. Sherrard had previously said: “During disciplinary proceedings we found Raj & Jai Construction did not have the governance or compliance systems in place we expect of a large builder in NSW.”
