World.title: This Sydney wedding venue wanted the pontoon. The locals weren’t having it
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life This Sydney wedding venue wanted the pontoon. The locals weren’t having it David Barwell August 25, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A pontoon along the popular Iron Cove Bay Run has become the latest flashpoint in a battle over the commercial use of Sydney’s public spaces after plans by a high-end function venue to use the structure for wedding ceremonies and bridal photographs prompted backlash from locals. After months of community opposition, Canada Bay Council has rejected a proposal by Drummoyne venue Aqua Luna to host weddings and events on the 15-metre pontoon, opposite its premises near the Iron Cove Bridge. The pontoon, which the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club uses to launch its boats. Andrew Quilty The decision delivered a significant victory to rowers, sporting groups, school students and residents who argued wedding events could restrict access for community members who use the pontoon daily, create safety risks and turn a structure designed for public use into a de facto private events space. On a Crown Land lease, Aqua Luna has been operating as a venue for weddings, functions and private events since 2017. It had proposed using the pontoon for gatherings of up to 50 guests during periods when there was no rowing.



The venue’s planning consultant, Peter Luff, said the proposal was aimed at strengthening Aqua Luna’s long-term viability, supporting local jobs and responding to growing demand for event spaces in Sydney. But the proposal met overwhelming community resistance – 98 per cent of submissions during public consultation opposed the plan. Drummoyne Rowing Club president Stephen Burke, left, with club patron Graham Wearne and rowers Amelia Cassidy and Emma Malka on the pontoon. Andrew Quilty Residents and sporting groups raised concerns about safety, public access and the compatibility of commercial wedding activities with the site’s status as Crown land zoned for “public recreation” and “environment protection”. Among the most vocal opponents was the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club, which operates from the lower level of the same building as Aqua Luna and relies on the pontoon as a key launching point.



Club president Stephen Burke warned wedding parties, photographers and event activity could interfere with rowing and create safety risks. “We’ve got more than 200 people rowing out of the shed, of all ages and abilities, and our concern is that allowing functions would have increased competition on the pontoon and caused serious problems,” he said. “The pontoon moves, it floats, it’s slippery – it’s simply not designed for weddings and just wouldn’t have worked.” Aqua Luna, which occupies the top floor of the same building as the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club. Andrew Quilty Tara Anglican School for Girls, which has used the pontoon for its rowing program for more than 25 years, cited what it described as “unacceptable safety risks” to students in opposing the application.



Rowing NSW and Sport NSW added support. Haberfield Rowing Club argued the proposal could set a precedent for the commercial use of community sporting infrastructure elsewhere in Sydney. The dispute comes as Sydney councils face increased pressure arising from commercial activities in public parks and other recreation spaces. In June, North Sydney Council introduced new permits and increased fees for some commercial operators, including wedding parties and fitness groups, amid concerns about the “privatisation” of public land. Canada Bay resident Phyllis Blennerhassett said public spaces are becoming increasingly important as Sydney’s population grows. “With a government push to increase housing density everywhere there’s increased demand for public recreation spaces like this and we have to protect them not just for us, but for the future,” she said.



Aqua Luna’s proposal prompted renewed scrutiny of its planning and regulation. Council records show the venue was granted development consent in 2016 on the condition it operated as a restaurant or cafe. However, council reports state the premise has since operated as a function centre without the necessary planning approval. As part of the latest application, Aqua Luna sought to regularise that use. Drummoyne Rowing Club rowers Emma Malka and Amelia Cassidy, president Stephen Burke and patron Graham Wearne. Andrew Quilty The issue was repeatedly raised during a Canada Bay Council meeting, as councillors questioned why the alleged non-compliance had continued for years without enforcement action. A council spokesman declined to answer questions about enforcement measures or whether any fines or infringement notices had been issued. Aqua Luna also declined to comment.



In a statement, the council said it would “work with the operator to ensure that the use of the premises is consistent with the development consent”. Canada Bay councillors voted on the proposal this week. Andrew Quilty After more than two hours of debate, councillors unanimously voted to reject the pontoon proposal but allowed the venue to continue operating a function centre as an “ancillary use” on the upper level of the building. The council will query the NSW government over the long-term future of the rowing club. Aqua Luna secured a 40-year extension of its Crown Lands lease of the site, extending its tenure into the 2070s. The rowing club’s existing lease, which operates through a sublease arrangement with Aqua Luna, is due to expire in 2034. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics Lisa Visentin August 25, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, the machines proved they are becoming faster, higher, and stronger, even as their practical utility beyond the athletics track remains uncertain. This is the second time China has hosted the games – an unofficial robot Olympics of its own making – which is designed to showcase its national talent against a backdrop of intensifying geopolitical rivalry in the high-tech sphere. Loading With the 100 metres sprint final still to go, the hot ticket is Chinese robot Tiangong Ultra. It took down Usain Bolt’s record in the heats on Saturday, clocking a 9.39-second dash and shaving 0.19 seconds off the Jamaican superstar’s time, which remains unbeaten by humans since 2009. The Tiangong team struck again on Sunday, claiming victory in the 400 metres final for both the small and large humanoid categories, the latter smashing a 2016 Olympic world record in the process.



If the competitors’ blank faces could express human emotion, they would surely depict sheer terror. The robots fanged it around the track with the unhinged gait of someone fleeing an axe murderer – staggering head forward, arms slicing wildly, on the cusp of falling with each step. Curious spectators have flocked to the National Speed Skating Oval, repurposed from the 2022 Winter Olympics, to watch the spectacle of humanoids competing across events including soccer, martial arts, tennis and athletics. This year’s competition added other scenario-based tests designed to demonstrate dexterity, such as block building, food preparation and storage packing. A humanoid robot falls to the ground before the competition starts the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Fairfax Media Robot teams face off in a soccer match. Fairfax Media Naturally, the games function as a giant marketing campaign for Chinese companies eager to attract the eyes (and wallets) of investors in what is a viciously competitive domestic sector already oversaturated with players. The future is clouded by strategic rivalry after the US banned the import of next-generation Chinese humanoids in a bid to protect its own nascent industry.



The events are less about the robots’ achievements on the day and more about signalling their future capabilities and commercial potential, which remain unclear for now. “I heard a robot ran faster than Bolt – that blew my mind,” says Li Ran, a 23-year-old university student who was watching the events with a friend. “If they get even more advanced and something bad happens, humans could be in serious danger.” For now, experts generally agree that humanoids are a long way from being autonomously deployed to carry out complex tasks in real-world environments. A humanoid robot developed by Galbot plays tennis against Chinese tennis star Zheng Jie at the games. Fairfax Media



We can – and maybe, in the name of scientific endeavour alone, we should – applaud man’s ingenuity in developing a lookalike machine that can now outrun man himself. Related Article China relations China is dominating the EV market. Now it wants to do the same with robots But when it comes to closing the capability gap between man and robot, perhaps the humanoids’ greatest achievement to date is their ability to reflect a collective exasperation with the human condition, with a distinctly 21st-century panache. Is there a more apt metaphor for existential futility than a humanoid sprinting at top speed in pursuit of man-made glory, only to fail to brake in time and slam into a safety barrier? And from there, stumble backwards, plough headfirst into the ground, and break at the waist, sending sparks shooting into the sky?



The Greeks had Sisyphus and his boulder. We have humanoids doomed to careen into walls on command. In a feat that launched a thousand memes, one robot did exactly this in the training heats before the games kicked off, giving the event’s promoters (the Chinese government) the hype and virality they were looking for. The competition has been joyously rich with crashes, face-plants, false starts and blowouts, the best ones sending limbs flying and requiring extinguishers for spot fires. Fallen comrades were carted off the tracks on blue stretchers. All of which makes the robot games a hoot, while injecting a degree of freewheeling chaos into Beijing’s image, otherwise better known for its staid and stage-managed public spectacles.



The concept of “world”, however, functions the same as it does in Major League Baseball’s World Series – a name suggestive of a greater level of international buy-in than it has. About 95 per cent of the 666 competing teams are Chinese, a share that mirrors China’s dominance in the global humanoid robotics sector. Despite their speed, the robots still lack the dexterity and finesse of their controllers. There will be no bidding war for the broadcast rights for humanoid soccer any time soon, unless there is a sudden explosion in demand for painfully slow midfield play, clunky defending, and goals that dribble over the line. Don’t take it from me. The kids of China’s Generation Alpha, the first digital natives to grow up in robotised megacities, are a little underwhelmed.



“Their reaction ability isn’t strong enough, so they miss chances. In terms of soccer performance, there’s still room for improvement,” says 12-year-old Zha Wenqi, who was watching with his dad. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: End of the ‘good bloke’ defence? WA’s plan to ban character references draws mixed response
World.content:
NationalWACourts End of the ‘good bloke’ defence? WA’s plan to ban character references draws mixed response Michael Philipps August 25, 2026 — 11:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government is set to announce a proposed blanket ban on character references at sentence hearings in a move that has drawn concern from the legal profession. WA Attorney General Tony Buti. Trevor Collens According to the state government, good character references will soon no longer be able to be used by courts as a mitigating factor at sentencing following landmark reforms set to be announced on Tuesday. The move comes after Western Power stood down three employees who provided glowing character references for a colleague who was convicted of raping a woman during a work trip. Jeffrey Spinner, 59, was convicted of four counts of sexual penetration without consent in April this year, and sentenced to five years jail.



He was found to have raped his colleague during a work trip after she became heavily intoxicated and vomited while the pair were having after-dinner drinks together. Related Article Courts Western Power stands down three employees for supporting rapist colleague During his sentencing, the court heard character references from five of his colleagues at Western Power, three men and two women. Western Power chief executive Gair Landsborough said the three employees in question were relieved of their duties and stood down as part of an internal review process. WA Attorney General Tony Buti said he had meetings with advocates for victim-survivors and heard how distressing it was when a criminal’s professional standing and community reputation were used to try to reduce their sentence.



“This is particularly distressing in cases of child abuse and sexual assault when a perpetrator’s friends and colleagues may be unaware of the perpetrator’s sinister behaviour,” he said. “This is important reform was already well advanced for child abuse cases, and expanding it to ban character references for other sentencing hearings is an important next step.” The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse recommended the removal of references in cases involving child abuse, however the state government has decided to expand this to all sentencing hearings. WA legal practitioners have labelled the proposed WA legislation an overreach by the government, arguing there is still a place for good character references in some cases. Perth Lawyer John Hammond character references had been a prominent part of the legal system for hundreds of years, and believed the blanket ban was “going in too hard.”



“The courts are very adept at taking into account the history of offenders and applying that to judgements,” he said. “Character references give the court an idea of how a sentence should be applied and also give a guide to how soon a person can be rehabilitated. “I certainly believe that it is appropriate when it comes to people convicted of sexual assault or child sex offences, but a complete ban on character references is a radical departure from a legal procedure that has been in place for hundreds of years.” The WA government is not the first state to try and implement a blanket ban. Earlier this year, the Victorian government announced it would remove the use of good character references at sentencing, although under the proposed legislation courts can still consider other factors when sentencing, including the chance of re-offending,



“Under our changes, courts will no longer consider evidence of ‘good character’ as a mitigating factor in sentencing,” a statement from the Victorian government read. “This already applies in some cases of child sexual abuse – our change will make it system-wide.” The Victorian bill was introduced this month and is currently progressing through the parliamentary stages. WA’s bill is being drafted.

World.title: The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview Jon Pierik August 25, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When James Hird said his goodbyes after finishing his challenging interview before the panel charged with finding Essendon’s new coach, he was buoyant. On two fronts. According to a senior industry figure with knowledge of the Bombers’ interviewing process, the former premiership captain and club great felt as if he had done all he could to reclaim a role he cherished, and one he had held proudly more than a decade ago before trouble struck. Mark McVeigh (left) and James Hird with the Bombers in 2004. Getty Images But, just as importantly, he was also satisfied the Bombers had run a thorough process, where he was given the freedom to push his case, but – on the flipside – was spared no leniency. That’s why, amid the disappointment of being overlooked in favour of great mate Mark McVeigh, Hird cannot complain.



“From a personal point of view though, it’s very disappointing,” Hird said on Nine’s Footy Furnace after it was confirmed that he, like Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide coaching director Murray Davis, had missed out on the job. “Yeah, I’m disappointed, put my heart and soul into the effort, but, obviously, fell short and that’s the way it goes.” Loading Before facing the selection committee of chief executive Tim Roberts, president Andrew Welsh, vice-president Anthony Di Pietro, board member and former Swans player Ted Richards and people and culture executive Caroline Monzon, Hird had felt the one issue that may torpedo his bid to return was the hangover from the supplements’ saga all those years ago, the same source said. However, Hird felt he had moved on as best he could. McVeigh was one of the 34 players suspended for the 2016 season. Over the years since, Hird has met with many of the 34 who had sought answers, and Hird provided them with as much clarity as he could.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unite behind our club’: Powerbroker’s call for peace as McVeigh appointed Essendon coach There were a couple who still harboured frustration, but Hird, according to the same senior source, had left those deep conversations believing the two parties were now on better terms. This process was relayed to Welsh when he asked Hird about his relationships with those former players, according to the same senior industry source. Welsh declined to discuss specifics of the interview when asked about this on Tuesday. Hird was pushed and challenged through the Bombers’ detailed process, as were all the candidates.



Late in his pivotal interview, Hird, according to two sources with knowledge of the meeting, asked the panel: “What concerns have you got about me being the coach?” Roberts said he had wondered whether Hird was “bigger than the club”. But Roberts and the rest of the panel agreed in the end that their concerns on that front had been extinguished. Ted Richards, the club’s football director, and a former teammate who went on to be a Sydney Swans’ premiership player, told Hird that successful coaches typically come from a top-four or top-six team and have experience at multiple clubs. Hird did not. Hird and McVeigh at Essendon in 2010. Getty Images Hird politely reminded the questioner that he had been captain of the best team of his era, the dominant 2000 premiership side, and, in his first stint as coach, the Bombers had played off for top spot on the ladder in round 14, 2013.



As this masthead has reported, Hird has also made it clear he had been involved in high-performance environments in the years since, including the business world, and you don’t need to follow the “typical linear” model to succeed. Hird had briefly been an assistant coach at Greater Western Sydney when McVeigh was caretaker coach, and is now director of coaching at VFL club, Port Melbourne. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move He had seen how the game – and coaching – had changed, the attention span of youngers players becoming shorter and shorter in this modern, social-media driven age. Rather than long sermons, Hird had seen the importance of sound-bites, and the use of artificial intelligence. Hird was asked how he would handle major media issues. The panel acknowledged that what Hird said, because of his huge standing in the game, let alone the club, carried tremendous weight, so if he broke ranks, the club could be destabilised.



Hird responded that he would always consult the president and chief executive, and would fall into line behind what the club wanted, regardless of his own view. Soccer great Kevin Muscat was used by the Bombers to scrutinise the applicants’ gameplan and strategy, although this was an open-ended question because applicants needed more details on the opponent they may have been playing and conditions at the venue. For anyone who has listened to Hird weekly on his football shows on Nine, the owner of this masthead, Hird has been big on having a team outnumber an opponent at the contest, and then run, spread and attack – as is the modern way. However, Welsh said McVeigh had the better plan. Andrew Welsh (second from left) and McVeigh (second from right) in their playing days. Paul Rovere “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage,” Welsh said.



“His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading.” Hird believed he was the best applicant for the job. As did all the applicants, otherwise why would they have applied? The Bombers may yet seek to bring him back inside the tent in a prominent role, but Hird craved the senior coaching role, and may be unwilling. Welsh said on Tuesday he was keen to catch up with Hird and would love to see him at Essendon in some capacity. A twist in the tale would be if Hird joined another club, raising eyebrows on Sunday when he said rivals had reached out to him. Hird has repeatedly said he wants what’s best for the Bombers, a one-time power that has fallen on hard and miserable times and just completed its worst season. As former club president Lindsay Tanner said, the job of all Essendon people now is to unite behind the new coach. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

Embattled western Sydney housing developer Bathla Group has collapsed into voluntary administration, leaving hundreds of buyers who purchased off-the-plan homes in limbo. Documents filed with the corporate regulator on Tuesday morning reveal Teneo has been appointed as administrator of the company, and its hundreds of related entities including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction. Bathla Group has collapsed. Louie Douvis In an Instagram post on the company’s page, founder and director Bhart Bhushan described the voluntary administration as the “orderly restructure of business” and blamed the decision on “a perfect storm” of declining sales, rising construction costs and the federal government’s May budget. “Our first thoughts are with our employees and the customers who have put their faith in us to deliver their dream of home ownership,” he said. “It is my sincere hope this process can allow that to happen by working collaboratively with the administrators, our suppliers, contractors and lending partners.”



In a statement, Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said the company recognised it was a “difficult situation” and said the appointment of administrators was “in the best interest of all stakeholders”. “The business has been through a period of declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased,” he said. “We will work constructively with the administrators to support the continued delivery of much-needed housing for western Sydney.” The collapse has left buyers who purchased off the plan unsure about what to do. Last week the Herald reported that buyers who had purchased apartments off the plan at Bathla’s Kembla Grange development had been unable to move in after the completion date for the project, which was originally slated for December 2025, had been extended four times. Janice Cahill, who bought an apartment at the development, said the delays have “really and truly” affected her mental health. When Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September last year, she found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces.



On Tuesday morning she called her real estate agent, asking what the collapse meant, and was assured the project was continuing. Building Commission NSW, the state’s construction watchdog, has undertaken more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites over the past few months. It identified defects at the Kembla Grange development. When asked why the completion date for the project had been pushed back, the spokesperson for Bathla said it was “due to unforeseen site delays with some external works … Completion is forecast for November”. Janice Cahill is hoping to move in to her new home later this year. It found the company had carried out work at two properties in Schofields without the mandatory Home Building Compensation Fund (HBCF) insurance being in place, and that its director, on behalf of Raj & Jai Construction, made misleading statements in the applications for the two HBCF insurance certificates. When the HBCF documentation for these properties was submitted in 2024, work had almost been completed, but the applications for the certificates stated that work was just beginning. Raj & Jai Construction was fined $45,000, and its director, $9000. “I accept that that’s not [a huge penalty] but these penalties were for these two particular offences and they were proportionate to those offences,” Building Commissioner James Sherrard told budget estimates on Monday. After months of community opposition, Canada Bay Council has rejected a proposal by Drummoyne venue Aqua Luna to host weddings and events on the 15-metre pontoon, opposite its premises near the Iron Cove Bridge. The pontoon, which the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club uses to launch its boats. Andrew Quilty The decision delivered a significant victory to rowers, sporting groups, school students and residents who argued wedding events could restrict access for community members who use the pontoon daily, create safety risks and turn a structure designed for public use into a de facto private events space. On a Crown Land lease, Aqua Luna has been operating as a venue for weddings, functions and private events since 2017. It had proposed using the pontoon for gatherings of up to 50 guests during periods when there was no rowing.



The venue’s planning consultant, Peter Luff, said the proposal was aimed at strengthening Aqua Luna’s long-term viability, supporting local jobs and responding to growing demand for event spaces in Sydney. But the proposal met overwhelming community resistance – 98 per cent of submissions during public consultation opposed the plan. Drummoyne Rowing Club president Stephen Burke, left, with club patron Graham Wearne and rowers Amelia Cassidy and Emma Malka on the pontoon. Andrew Quilty Residents and sporting groups raised concerns about safety, public access and the compatibility of commercial wedding activities with the site’s status as Crown land zoned for “public recreation” and “environment protection”. Among the most vocal opponents was the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club, which operates from the lower level of the same building as Aqua Luna and relies on the pontoon as a key launching point.



Club president Stephen Burke warned wedding parties, photographers and event activity could interfere with rowing and create safety risks. “We’ve got more than 200 people rowing out of the shed, of all ages and abilities, and our concern is that allowing functions would have increased competition on the pontoon and caused serious problems,” he said. “The pontoon moves, it floats, it’s slippery – it’s simply not designed for weddings and just wouldn’t have worked.” Aqua Luna, which occupies the top floor of the same building as the 107-year-old Drummoyne Rowing Club. Andrew Quilty Tara Anglican School for Girls, which has used the pontoon for its rowing program for more than 25 years, cited what it described as “unacceptable safety risks” to students in opposing the application.



Rowing NSW and Sport NSW added support. Haberfield Rowing Club argued the proposal could set a precedent for the commercial use of community sporting infrastructure elsewhere in Sydney. The dispute comes as Sydney councils face increased pressure arising from commercial activities in public parks and other recreation spaces. In June, North Sydney Council introduced new permits and increased fees for some commercial operators, including wedding parties and fitness groups, amid concerns about the “privatisation” of public land. Canada Bay resident Phyllis Blennerhassett said public spaces are becoming increasingly important as Sydney’s population grows. “With a government push to increase housing density everywhere there’s increased demand for public recreation spaces like this and we have to protect them not just for us, but for the future,” she said.



Aqua Luna’s proposal prompted renewed scrutiny of its planning and regulation. Council records show the venue was granted development consent in 2016 on the condition it operated as a restaurant or cafe. However, council reports state the premise has since operated as a function centre without the necessary planning approval. As part of the latest application, Aqua Luna sought to regularise that use. Drummoyne Rowing Club rowers Emma Malka and Amelia Cassidy, president Stephen Burke and patron Graham Wearne. Andrew Quilty The issue was repeatedly raised during a Canada Bay Council meeting, as councillors questioned why the alleged non-compliance had continued for years without enforcement action. A council spokesman declined to answer questions about enforcement measures or whether any fines or infringement notices had been issued. Aqua Luna also declined to comment.



In a statement, the council said it would “work with the operator to ensure that the use of the premises is consistent with the development consent”. Canada Bay councillors voted on the proposal this week. Andrew Quilty After more than two hours of debate, councillors unanimously voted to reject the pontoon proposal but allowed the venue to continue operating a function centre as an “ancillary use” on the upper level of the building. The council will query the NSW government over the long-term future of the rowing club. Aqua Luna secured a 40-year extension of its Crown Lands lease of the site, extending its tenure into the 2070s. The rowing club’s existing lease, which operates through a sublease arrangement with Aqua Luna, is due to expire in 2034. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics
World.content:
Analysis WorldAsiaChina relations Records tumble and so do robots at China’s humanoid Olympics Lisa Visentin August 25, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: At the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, the machines proved they are becoming faster, higher, and stronger, even as their practical utility beyond the athletics track remains uncertain. This is the second time China has hosted the games – an unofficial robot Olympics of its own making – which is designed to showcase its national talent against a backdrop of intensifying geopolitical rivalry in the high-tech sphere. Loading With the 100 metres sprint final still to go, the hot ticket is Chinese robot Tiangong Ultra. It took down Usain Bolt’s record in the heats on Saturday, clocking a 9.39-second dash and shaving 0.19 seconds off the Jamaican superstar’s time, which remains unbeaten by humans since 2009. The Tiangong team struck again on Sunday, claiming victory in the 400 metres final for both the small and large humanoid categories, the latter smashing a 2016 Olympic world record in the process.



If the competitors’ blank faces could express human emotion, they would surely depict sheer terror. The robots fanged it around the track with the unhinged gait of someone fleeing an axe murderer – staggering head forward, arms slicing wildly, on the cusp of falling with each step. Curious spectators have flocked to the National Speed Skating Oval, repurposed from the 2022 Winter Olympics, to watch the spectacle of humanoids competing across events including soccer, martial arts, tennis and athletics. This year’s competition added other scenario-based tests designed to demonstrate dexterity, such as block building, food preparation and storage packing. A humanoid robot falls to the ground before the competition starts the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. Fairfax Media Robot teams face off in a soccer match. Fairfax Media Naturally, the games function as a giant marketing campaign for Chinese companies eager to attract the eyes (and wallets) of investors in what is a viciously competitive domestic sector already oversaturated with players. The future is clouded by strategic rivalry after the US banned the import of next-generation Chinese humanoids in a bid to protect its own nascent industry.



The events are less about the robots’ achievements on the day and more about signalling their future capabilities and commercial potential, which remain unclear for now. “I heard a robot ran faster than Bolt – that blew my mind,” says Li Ran, a 23-year-old university student who was watching the events with a friend. “If they get even more advanced and something bad happens, humans could be in serious danger.” For now, experts generally agree that humanoids are a long way from being autonomously deployed to carry out complex tasks in real-world environments. A humanoid robot developed by Galbot plays tennis against Chinese tennis star Zheng Jie at the games. Fairfax Media



We can – and maybe, in the name of scientific endeavour alone, we should – applaud man’s ingenuity in developing a lookalike machine that can now outrun man himself. Related Article China relations China is dominating the EV market. Now it wants to do the same with robots But when it comes to closing the capability gap between man and robot, perhaps the humanoids’ greatest achievement to date is their ability to reflect a collective exasperation with the human condition, with a distinctly 21st-century panache. Is there a more apt metaphor for existential futility than a humanoid sprinting at top speed in pursuit of man-made glory, only to fail to brake in time and slam into a safety barrier? And from there, stumble backwards, plough headfirst into the ground, and break at the waist, sending sparks shooting into the sky?



The Greeks had Sisyphus and his boulder. We have humanoids doomed to careen into walls on command. In a feat that launched a thousand memes, one robot did exactly this in the training heats before the games kicked off, giving the event’s promoters (the Chinese government) the hype and virality they were looking for. The competition has been joyously rich with crashes, face-plants, false starts and blowouts, the best ones sending limbs flying and requiring extinguishers for spot fires. Fallen comrades were carted off the tracks on blue stretchers. All of which makes the robot games a hoot, while injecting a degree of freewheeling chaos into Beijing’s image, otherwise better known for its staid and stage-managed public spectacles.



The concept of “world”, however, functions the same as it does in Major League Baseball’s World Series – a name suggestive of a greater level of international buy-in than it has. About 95 per cent of the 666 competing teams are Chinese, a share that mirrors China’s dominance in the global humanoid robotics sector. Despite their speed, the robots still lack the dexterity and finesse of their controllers. There will be no bidding war for the broadcast rights for humanoid soccer any time soon, unless there is a sudden explosion in demand for painfully slow midfield play, clunky defending, and goals that dribble over the line. Don’t take it from me. The kids of China’s Generation Alpha, the first digital natives to grow up in robotised megacities, are a little underwhelmed.



“Their reaction ability isn’t strong enough, so they miss chances. In terms of soccer performance, there’s still room for improvement,” says 12-year-old Zha Wenqi, who was watching with his dad. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: End of the ‘good bloke’ defence? WA’s plan to ban character references draws mixed response
World.content:
NationalWACourts End of the ‘good bloke’ defence? WA’s plan to ban character references draws mixed response Michael Philipps August 25, 2026 — 11:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government is set to announce a proposed blanket ban on character references at sentence hearings in a move that has drawn concern from the legal profession. WA Attorney General Tony Buti. Trevor Collens According to the state government, good character references will soon no longer be able to be used by courts as a mitigating factor at sentencing following landmark reforms set to be announced on Tuesday. The move comes after Western Power stood down three employees who provided glowing character references for a colleague who was convicted of raping a woman during a work trip. Jeffrey Spinner, 59, was convicted of four counts of sexual penetration without consent in April this year, and sentenced to five years jail.



He was found to have raped his colleague during a work trip after she became heavily intoxicated and vomited while the pair were having after-dinner drinks together. Related Article Courts Western Power stands down three employees for supporting rapist colleague During his sentencing, the court heard character references from five of his colleagues at Western Power, three men and two women. Western Power chief executive Gair Landsborough said the three employees in question were relieved of their duties and stood down as part of an internal review process. WA Attorney General Tony Buti said he had meetings with advocates for victim-survivors and heard how distressing it was when a criminal’s professional standing and community reputation were used to try to reduce their sentence.



“This is particularly distressing in cases of child abuse and sexual assault when a perpetrator’s friends and colleagues may be unaware of the perpetrator’s sinister behaviour,” he said. “This is important reform was already well advanced for child abuse cases, and expanding it to ban character references for other sentencing hearings is an important next step.” The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse recommended the removal of references in cases involving child abuse, however the state government has decided to expand this to all sentencing hearings. WA legal practitioners have labelled the proposed WA legislation an overreach by the government, arguing there is still a place for good character references in some cases. Perth Lawyer John Hammond character references had been a prominent part of the legal system for hundreds of years, and believed the blanket ban was “going in too hard.”



“The courts are very adept at taking into account the history of offenders and applying that to judgements,” he said. “Character references give the court an idea of how a sentence should be applied and also give a guide to how soon a person can be rehabilitated. “I certainly believe that it is appropriate when it comes to people convicted of sexual assault or child sex offences, but a complete ban on character references is a radical departure from a legal procedure that has been in place for hundreds of years.” The WA government is not the first state to try and implement a blanket ban. Earlier this year, the Victorian government announced it would remove the use of good character references at sentencing, although under the proposed legislation courts can still consider other factors when sentencing, including the chance of re-offending,



“Under our changes, courts will no longer consider evidence of ‘good character’ as a mitigating factor in sentencing,” a statement from the Victorian government read. “This already applies in some cases of child sexual abuse – our change will make it system-wide.” The Victorian bill was introduced this month and is currently progressing through the parliamentary stages. WA’s bill is being drafted.
